articles.title: Lebanese sceptical Israeli polls will bring change, end occupation of south
articles.summary: Residents and analysts doubt October 27 vote will bring any meaningful shift in Israeli policy towards their country.
articles.body:
Beirut, Lebanon – As Israel’s October 27 election nears, so does the possibility that the government that has overseen the invasion and reoccupation of southern Lebanon could be deposed.

But for people in Lebanon, optimism that a change in the Israeli government will bode well for Israel’s neighbours is low .

“I don’t think anything major – or at all – will change for Lebanon even if there’s a change in [Israeli] leadership,” said Beirut resident Fouad Debs.

“Any internal change might lead to small, insignificant changes just to show the outside world that Israeli society and politics are not messed up or evil,” added the lawyer.

For many in Lebanon, Israel’s history of airspace violations, ground invasions and occupation has led to a general atmosphere of distrust, regardless of who is in charge of the country.

“Proof is what people [in Israel] are saying as the elections [approach],” said Karim Safieddine, a Beirut-based nonresident fellow at the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy.

“No one is promising withdrawal, and no one is addressing south Lebanon as a crisis or a mistake,” he added, noting that the “general Israeli establishment looks at Lebanon as its prize”.

Israel and the Lebanese Shia group Hezbollah have been fighting, with different levels of intensity, since October 2023 in the wake of the Hamas-led attack in southern Israel and Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip that followed it. Israel has twice escalated the conflict – first in September 2024 and then in March this year, following the start of the United States-Israeli war on Iran.

In June, following direct negotations that were rejected by Hezbollah, Israel and the Lebanese government signed a US-brokered framework agreement that included the goal of securing the phased withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanon. Still, Israel continues to occupy large parts of its neighbour’s south, where it has systematically demolished homes and infrastructure in dozens of villages, forcing more than one million people from their homes.

Lebanese generally disagree on how to deal with Israel, as shown by a June 2026 survey by Lebanese American University professor Jad Melki and his team.

In the study, 54 percent of Lebanese polled said they supported diplomacy with Israel, while 35 percent preferred armed resistance. But the poll also found that regardless of the tactic, Lebanese views of Israel were overwhelmingly negative, with 87 percent of those polled considering it “as their enemy”.

In next week’s polls, the primary challenge to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – the man who has overseen Israel’s war on Lebanon that has killed almost 9,000 people since October 2023, including journalists, first responders and children – appears to be Gadi Eisenkot , the leader of the Yashar party.

Many Israelis see Eisenkot as a break from Netanyahu, who has been inundated with corruption trials , accusations of failure to prevent a Hamas-led attack in October 2023 and of prioritising attacking Gaza over releasing Israeli captives .

But in Lebanon, the general feeling is that whoever replaces Netanyahu is unlikely to deviate from the current policy of occupation and destruction.

Eisenkot, in particular, is a former general and chief of staff in the Israeli army with a historical impact on Lebanon. He acted as northern front commander in Israel’s 2006 war on Lebanon and is the architect of the Dahiyeh Doctrine, an Israeli military strategy of using disproportionate damage and destruction currently being used by Israel in Gaza and Lebanon.

More recently, he has accused Netanyahu of giving in to US pressure by stopping attacks on Beirut since April, arguing that the Israeli military should attack Hezbollah targets anywhere in Lebanon.

Lebanese analysts said that, although Netanyahu is wanted by the International Criminal Court on charges of war crimes in Gaza, Eisenkot and other challengers have mostly attacked him on domestic issues and from the right , calling him soft on issues of security.

“Those that have come forward as candidates in Israeli elections criticise Netanyahu and his handling of the war,” Elia Ayoub, a Lebanese researcher and podcaster, told Al Jazeera. “They’re not criticising him based on any kind of humanitarianism or anything [related to] human rights.”

Ayoub said the attitude towards Lebanon and other peoples and countries in the region goes beyond the Netanyahu government. He pointed out the governmental and societal backlash to the recent release of NAZA, a documentary made by Israeli journalists in which Israeli soldiers speak about the calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza.

“There’s a profoundly dehumanising discourse that is completely normalised in Israeli society, and the backlash against any pushback is drastic,” said Ayoub. “I don’t necessarily believe that it’s going to change Israeli policy towards Lebanon.”

Since the June trilateral framework agreement, Lebanon appears stuck in a limbo. While active fighting between the two sides has largely stopped, Israel continues its demolition campaign with little opposition. As the occupation becomes increasingly entrenched, many Lebanese fear it could last another generation .

“Definitely, it’s a prolonged situation of neither war nor peace,” said Safieddine. “We’re going to be living in this grey area for a very long time.”

With next week’s election unlikely to bring any meaningful change to Israel’s policies towards Lebanon and the wider region, Ayoub stressed the importance of the midterm polls in the US on November 3.

“The US elections are just as important, if not more important,” he said, “because they tend to determine how much the Israelis feel emboldened toward Palestinians first and foremost, but of course, towards Lebanon as well, and Syria to a large extent.”

articles.title: Brazil election: How a changing working class is reshaping the presidential race
articles.summary: Calls for change present a challenge to President Lula in the second round of the election on Sunday.
articles.body:
In the sprawling former industrial city of Osasco, shuttered factories have given way to a shopping malls and delivery app tech companies in what is now dubbed São Paulo's "Silicon Valley."

The municipality voted for Brazil's left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in 2022 but switched to the right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round of Brazil's presidential election this month. Bolsonaro won that vote - and now the two men face a run-off on Sunday. Since 1989, every first-round winner has gone on to be elected president.

Like many of Lula's traditional supporters, Gilberto Almazan, who leads a metalworkers' union here, is visibly worried.

He cries when he tells Lula's life story: a boy who grew up in hunger in the north-east, who became a metalworker, then a union leader, then a three-time president. But he's candid about how things have changed here and how the union movement that was so integral to Lula's support base is stuck in the "Middle Ages", and struggling to keep up.

"We had strong deindustrialisation here," Almazan says. "The profile of the working class changed. They are no longer predominantly industrial workers, they are service workers.

"Metal, chemical, textile factories disappeared. And five malls were built."

The word "change" comes up repeatedly among Bolsonaro supporters here. Many struggle to name specific Bolsonaro policies they like but know they want to try something different: frustrated by the economy, crime and corruption in politics – even though Flávio has been faced accusations of corruption too, which he denies.

"He brings the hope of change, that we can have a different Brazil," says lawyer Gisele Bonfim in Osasco, who decided to vote for Bolsonaro after supporting Lula in 2022.

Lula's re-election campaign has been hampered by voters turning away from him. In some cases, their frustration drove abstention, which was higher than average this year, but others like Gisele actively wanted something new.

One major reason for that is Brazil's working class has transformed seismically in places like Osasco.

Near one large shopping mall lies an open-air market where this shift is noticeable. Everyone is touting products, armed with a portable card machine.

Tairine, who sells hot dogs, used to abstain from voting, even though - as voting is compulsory in Brazil - not going to the polls incurs a fine. This year, she plans to vote for Bolsonaro. She points to high taxes paid on "everything" she buys and says these make it "so difficult for a poor person" dealing with inflation, arguing "nothing has changed" since Lula became president again.

Flávio Bolsonaro has proposed cutting government spending, government ministries, and some taxes - though he has said he'd maintain some of Lula's flagship welfare programmes.

For his supporters, Lula is a working-class hero credited with advancing workers' rights through organising strikes and lifting millions of people out of poverty with generous social welfare programmes as president.

But across Brazil millions now work in the gig economy, a phenomenon Almazan calls "Uber-isation": driving for Uber, delivering food, or running small businesses from market stalls to providing at-home beauty treatments.

"There are a lot of workers who need more freedom, flexibility of days and hours," he says, rather than the welfare and collective action Lula offered.

Richard Lapper, who has written biographies of both Lula and Jair Bolsonaro – Flavio's father and Brazil's president from 2019-2022 - says the rise of individualised work and the decline of manufacturing caused by globalisation are not unique to Brazil.

But because Brazil industrialised late and deindustrialised early, he argues, the effects have been sharper here. He calls Lula a "victim of his own success."

Unemployment fell to a record low, and Brazil was taken off the UN's Hunger Map during Lula's current presidency. But Lapper describes a crisis of "expectations" in which people are now better off but don't feel it because prices have risen and household debt and interest rates are high.

Robson, 53, is a municipal civil servant in Osasco. Originally from Lula's north-eastern home state of Pernambuco, he grew up supporting him.

But he describes a country now running deficits and says its citizens are enduring the "worst phase" of its tax burden, which he blames on the Lula government's "mismanagement" of the economy and high public spending.

"Now you have to make choices: pay an instalment for your car, or put food on the table," he says.

In some areas, Lula lost votes compared to 2022, even though Bolsonaro did not gain more than his father did then: 33 million people did not vote in the first round, the highest abstention since 1998.

In response, Lula's campaign has focused on mobilising hundreds of thousands of people – particularly students – on to the streets to get the vote out for round two. It claims one rally in São Paulo attracted about a million people.

"A lot of people didn't vote, they thought it wouldn't change anything," says one supporter, Leila. "Our fight is to make those people believe their vote changes things."

Aerial videos of these huge demonstrations have been plastered across social media. An image of a topless man with a six-pack waving a Lula flag at one has been shared tens of millions of times.

The strategy is that their revolution will not be televised, but it should ideally go viral.

Lula, 80, has also been using social media to dismiss criticisms that he is past his prime: calling himself the "king of selfies" and posting videos showing him running from A to B on the campaign trail.

In Maré, one of Rio's largest favelas which is controlled by rival gangs, abstention was higher than average.

This dented Lula's support, even though he still won here: among Brazil's very poorest, Lula's welfare initiatives clearly do still resonate. One 18-year-old mother in Maré, Vitoria, earns less than £300 a month and praises Lula's government for increasing the minimum wage, giving workers the right to two days off, and providing essential medicines for free.

She is sceptical of Bolsonaro's plans to designate the gang which controls this part of the favela, Comando Vermelho, as a terrorist organisation, which he lobbied the US to do earlier this year.

She thinks it will lead to authorities entering the favela to "kill, destroy, ruin families, leave blood and bodies on the ground", citing a police raid in Rio last year that killed more than 130 people.

Another resident, Andreza Dionísio, blames high abstention rates here on both last-minute changes to polling station locations, but also "a sense of hopelessness about the future."

Increasingly, that void of hope is being filled by the growth of the evangelical church: about a quarter of Brazilians are now evangelical. Its mega-churches offer not just a spiritual home but support with issues like childcare, employment advice and even food.

Its conservative pastors are some of Brazil's most powerful political operators.

Silas Malafaia, who has millions of followers on social media, leads the Assembleia de Deus Vitória em Cristo headquartered in the lower middle-class neighbourhood of Penha in Rio de Janeiro. He is being investigated for allegedly obstructing the coup trial of Jair Bolsonaro, which he denies and calls politically motivated.

At one two-hour sermon he preaches messages of self-improvement to an emotional crowd of hundreds, interrupted occasionally for live music interludes and breaks to collect money with card machines. The whole event is live-streamed on YouTube.

Afterwards, in his office adorned with a photo of him and the former president Jair Bolsonaro, at whose wedding he officiated, he told the BBC that without the evangelical church in working-class neighbourhoods the country would be "in a state worse than you can imagine".

"It gives these people meaning. To better their lives."

He argues Flávio Bolsonaro shares the church's values: for family, and against gender "ideology" and abortion.

The church is driving some to actively vote for Flávio Bolsonaro, but among much of Brazil's new working class, the first round feels more like a rejection of President Lula than an endorsement of his rival.

"There will never be another Lula," Gilberto Almazan fears. He intends this as a compliment, but Brazil's changing world of work means it's also probably true.

While Lula's past story still stirs great emotion for people like Almazan, his political fate may depend on whether voters think he can now offer Brazil a new one.

articles.summary: Shopkeepers in Paris are boarding up windows and securing their premises ahead of fresh anti-government protests scheduled across France on Saturday, a
articles.body: Shopkeepers in Paris are boarding up windows and securing their premises ahead of fresh anti-government protests scheduled across France on Saturday, a week after demonstrations escalated into violent riots that left thousands of businesses vandalised or looted.The unrest last weekend saw more than 2,500 people arrested across the country, while the French government said around 450 shops in Paris alone were damaged or looted.Businesses are now preparing for possible further disruption as authorities step up security measures and demonstrations are planned in several cities.At Place de la République in central Paris, shopfronts were left with shattered windows, graffiti-covered walls and burnt-out kiosks and bus shelters after the previous weekend's violence.Restaurant owner Abdul Mahmoud was quoted by NPR as saying that he watched in horror as people broke into his establishment, took drinks and emptied cash registers.“We all have a right to protest,” he said, “but vandalism, that's a different matter.”Shopkeepers take precautions as demonstrations approachBusinesses in Paris are preparing for the possibility of renewed violence, while shopkeepers in other French cities are also reinforcing their premises.In Lyon, workers were seen installing wooden panels and protective fencing outside City Hall, the Museum of Fine Arts and the Chamber of Commerce on Friday, Euronews reported.Shops along Rue de la République were also securing their windows with wooden boards.In Orléans, businesses along the planned protest route have taken similar precautions ahead of a weekend that will see the city host a congress of the far-right National Rally party.Around 20,000 to 30,000 protesters are expected to gather in opposition to the event, with nearly 3,000 police officers and security personnel due to be deployed, according to Euronews.The preparations come amid fears of further property damage.France deploys 70,000 police officersInterior minister Laurent Nuñez said around 70,000 police officers and gendarmes would be deployed across France over the weekend. The move follows criticism of the authorities' response to last weekend's unrest.“We will not let anything go unchallenged,” Nuñez said.He also warned that the government would be “uncompromising with the vandals, with the looters, and all those who commit acts of violence”.Authorities have imposed restrictions on demonstrations in several cities. French President Emmanuel Macron decreed earlier in the week that only demonstrations organised by recognised trade unions would be permitted on Saturday, while cities including Lyon, Nice and Montpellier announced broader bans on gatherings.Despite the restrictions, hundreds of demonstrations and other actions were planned across the country. A student union-led march in Paris was ordered to follow a route away from the city centre.The Louvre, Orsay and Picasso museums were due to close on Saturday, while a scheduled home match for football club Paris Saint-Germain was moved to Monday.Student protests widen amid cost-of-living angerThe protests began last month when high school students mobilised over conditions in schools.They subsequently expanded to include wider groups protesting against the rising cost of living.While some demonstrators have condemned looting and vandalism, others have defended the protests as a means of expressing anger over the government's policies.Nicolas Fournier, a 25-year-old who works at a cafe in Place de la République, told NPR that he supported the protests and was sympathetic towards some of those involved in looting.“People who steal, they are just getting what they didn't get from the government. I'm not mad at them at all,” he said, describing the moment as historic.“I think we're in a second French Revolution,” Fournier added.Macron met representatives of high school students on Friday ahead of the demonstrations. Although the representatives said he had made commitments to them, they urged students to continue mobilising.The unrest has also intensified political tensions ahead of France's 2027 presidential election.The National Rally's congress in Orléans is expected to draw thousands of party supporters, while left-wing groups are planning counter-protests.Authorities are now preparing for demonstrations across the country while businesses take precautions against a repeat of last weekend's destruction.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2023, archaeologist Michael Fradley reported spotting three Roman camps while surveying satellite images for Oxford’s EAMENA project; they may reveal a military campaign into Arabia missing from surviving histories
articles.summary: Archaeologist Michael Fradley uncovers three Roman camps in Saudi Arabia, revealing evidence of a lost military campaign previously undocumented in history. This discovery, part of Oxford's EAMENA project, challenges perceptions of Roman expansion into the Nabataean Kingdom.
articles.body: At the University of Oxford, a team that records endangered heritage sites across the Middle East and North Africa used freely available satellite images to find and document archaeological remains. Oxford attributed the discovery to Michael Fradley, who first spotted a faint rectangular outline on Google Earth while the team was exploring the border zone between southern Jordan and Saudi Arabia. It was a typical formation of Roman soldiers' enclosures, which were erected when troops were on the march. An investigation of the nearby terrain revealed additional formations in a similar direction.Roman literature contains nothing about any large-scale military action during the conquest of the Nabataean Kingdom and it has traditionally been considered a relatively peaceful operation. Temporary encampments are the type of construction an army leaves behind during a march, so a line of them running far into the desert suggests a previously undocumented expedition, although the western camp’s larger size means the three camps cannot yet be assumed to have held one uniform force. This is what the researchers define as a hypothesis, because the construction has not been excavated or examined yet.The EAMENA survey and the three camps east of BayirThe EAMENA website states that the Endangered Archaeology in the Middle East and North Africa project was set up in 2015 and that its team uses satellite imagery, aerial photography and on-the-ground visits to record archaeological sites and assess their condition. The findings were published in Antiquity in the study A lost campaign? New evidence of Roman temporary camps in northern Arabia, by Michael Fradley, Andrew Wilson, Bill Finlayson and Robert Bewley. Oxford’s research archive lists the publication date as 27 April 2023, which matches the online publication date shown on the paper’s Cambridge University Press page.The paper says remote sensing in southern Jordan identified at least three Roman temporary camps east of Bayir, with the western camp covering roughly 1.291 hectares. The authors argue the alignment points to an expedition toward Dûmat al-Jandal and may fit the Roman annexation of the Nabataean kingdom after AD 106. There are three camps to the east of the settlement of Bayir, located in a row leading to Dûmat al-Jandal in the Jawf region of Saudi Arabia. They have been recognized by the research group as possible Roman temporary camps due to their playing card shape, their symmetrical entrance and the tituli placed in front of the entrances.Camp dimensions and the 1982 and 2017 satellite imagesThe heritage news website, The Past, says the western camp spans approximately 125 by 105 metres, while the central and eastern camps each span around 95 by 65 metres. The above-mentioned study places the eastern camp 37.7 kilometres east-southeast of the central camp. The satellite image of the eastern camp provided by Google Earth and Maxar in The Past is dated 26 February 2017. However, since most of the land has been converted to central-pivot irrigation, the researchers also used the Kh9 Hexagon imagery dated 24 August 1982. This imagery did not show any additional camps, although the paper notes that further camps east of the easternmost camp may have been lost under wind-blown sands. The paper adds that the Aerial Archaeology in Jordan project later photographed the western and central camps from the air. This discovery is rare. An earlier review by Kennedy, cited in the paper, identified only four possible Roman temporary camps in Jordan.Why the camps may belong to the Nabataean annexation of AD 106The transfer of power after the death of the last Nabataean king, Rabbel II Soter, in AD 106 is usually seen as peaceful because Roman literature mentions no major military campaign, as The Past explains. The camps paint a different picture. In its news release on the discovery, the University of Oxford reports Professor Andrew Wilson, a co-author of the paper, as saying that the camps suggest the annexation was not entirely straightforward and that Rome moved quickly to secure the kingdom, if the early second-century dating is correct.The authors of the above-mentioned study suggest that further investigation near Dumat al-Jandal and Sakaka, which could have been the goal of the campaign, might reveal more about the Roman army in the region. The same study considers the annexation by the emperor Trajan after AD 106 the most plausible time frame for the expedition, but calls it a hypothesis because the camps cannot yet be dated.Roman troops at Hegra and the questions still openOther sources indicate the operation of Rome in the area. "The Roman Military Camp in Ancient Hegra" is written by Zbigniew Fiema and François Villeneuve, published in 2018 in the proceedings of the 23rd International Limes Congress. In the paper, it is stated that the annexation of Trajan in AD 106 added Hegra, located in northwestern Saudi Arabia, along with northern Hijaz, to the province of Arabia; there are also some inscriptions about Roman forces located there. The Antiquity article notes that the Roman army was present as far south as Hegra by AD 175, but argues that Roman control of the area was long established by then, which makes that period a less convincing setting for the campaign than Trajan’s annexation after AD 106. Still, questions regarding the new camps are to be resolved. In comments for Sky News, Dr. Wilson expressed his surprise about why the western camp might be almost twice as spacious as the other two camps. The Jerusalem Post reports possible explanations, including that the garrison may have been smaller or that the camp may have supported the others with water supplies.You use AI every day. articles.title: How Benjamin Netanyahu reshaped Israel’s institutions
articles.summary: As Israel heads to the polls on October 27, its polarising and longest-serving prime minister is seeking re-election.
articles.body:
To his supporters, he is known as “King Bibi”; but to his opponents, he is the king of security failures and corruption.

Disputes over names aside, what is not in question is that Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, has left his mark on the country’s institutions, politics and social attitudes during a decades-long career that has been defined by Israel’s lurch to the right.

As he seeks re-election in Israel’s October 27 polls, analysts say his most enduring domestic legacy may be the right-wing, militaristic opposition that he has helped create and now faces.

Born in 1949, Netanyahu entered Israel’s central political stage in the early 1990s by fuelling anger at possible peace deals with the Palestinians and Syria.

Israeli political leaders have accused him of leading incitement that motivated the 1995 assassination of then-Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, who was leading negotiations with the Palestine Liberation Organization, by an ultranationalist Israeli. Netanyahu had led rallies in which participants depicted Rabin in a Nazi SS uniform and held signs of him in the crosshairs of a gun, while others shouted “traitor”.

The Likud Party leader denies any responsibility, but former security officials have said they warned Netanyahu before the assassination and asked him to dial down his rhetoric, only for him to refuse, according to Israeli media reports.

In 1996, Netanyahu’s populist tactics succeeded at the ballot box, making him Israel’s youngest prime minister. Netanyahu’s transactional leadership style gave prominence to extreme-right and religious parties that are now an indispensable part of his right-wing alliance.

Under him, religious courts have expanded powers, including over civil and business disputes. State institutions accommodate religious agendas and allocate record levels of funding to ultra-Orthodox schools and institutions.

Netanyahu inscribed his political ideology, especially on the identity of the state and the status of Palestinian citizens of Israel, into law. In 2018, the Knesset passed the so-called Nation-State Basic Law , which states – among other things – that Israel is the exclusive state of the Jewish people and also makes advancing illegal settlements a national priority.

Human rights organisations in Israel petitioned the High Court to stop the legislation from going into effect, but the petition was rejected. International experts and rights groups cite this law, among others, as evidence of Israel committing the crime of apartheid in its treatment of Palestinians.

Netanyahu also re-engineered state institutions, including Israel’s security structures, appointing loyalists and political allies to senior positions. He also clashed with security chiefs that he deemed antagonistic. And in the aftermath of the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack, which triggered Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, Netanyahu deflected blame and responsibility on the security establishment, prompting Ronen Bar, who was the Shin Bet chief in 2023, to sue him for defamation.

A major change to Israeli institutions that was spearheaded by Netanyahu during his 19 on-and-off years in power affected the judiciary, which is examining lingering corruption charges that could see him serve time in prison if he is convicted. Netanyahu, who is up against three separate cases of corruption filed in 2019, denies any wrongdoing.

Under his leadership, the Knesset adopted legislation that changed the composition of the Judicial Selection Committee to ensure greater political influence for the governing coalition.

Netanyahu called it “judicial reform” to stop what he often calls a “judicial dictatorship” ruling over elected officials.

Opponents called it a “coup” that sparked wide-scale protests : a push to curtail the independence of the High Court and give politicians influence over the courts and ministerial legal advisers.

In line with his efforts to subvert independent oversight, Netanyahu tried repeatedly, but unsuccessfully, to fire the attorney general.

But he succeeded in dismissing the military’s advocate general for leaking a video of Israeli soldiers gang-raping a Palestinian detainee. The soldiers were also released and cleared of charges.

At the same time, Netanyahu is dogged by corruption cases dating back to 2019, which could see him serve time in prison if convicted

The prime minister, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court on charges of war crimes in Gaza, says his work is not over. He promises his supporters he will complete the overhaul of judicial review and press on with other highly controversial policies.

Netanyahu’s supporters and allies view him as a leader who delivers, and one who achieved what others could not. His opponents pledge to undo the damage Netanyahu caused over the past decades, pointing to corruption, social divisions and increasing international isolation as outcomes of his rule.

But undoing such formative changes, many of which are now law, may be easier said than done.

articles.title: Junior Eurovision 2026: Ireland's duo takes the stage in Malta
articles.summary: Ireland's representatives contain 13-year-old Naomi from Mayobridge, County Down.
articles.body:
They both feel comfortably at home in the spotlight, but as they prepare for the biggest show of their young lives, Ireland's junior Eurovision singers admit some nerves are creeping in.

Junior Eurovision Song Contest 2026 will be held on Saturday in Malta.

Ireland's representatives feature Naomi, 13, from Mayobridge, County Down and 14-year-old Caleb from Dublin. They are the contest's only duo.

They are among 15 other nations that will compete to win the contest, which will be staged under the theme The Festa, a vibrant celebration of Malta's village tradition.

The running order for Saturday's show has already been drawn, with the Irish act the 13th to perform.

Naomi is at home in the spotlight. Singing runs in her family, inherited from her nanny and grandad.

The 13-year-old is no stranger to the stage, and it's where she feels most at home, however she can't help but feel a little bit of nerves ahead of Saturday.

"We are definitely a wee bit nervous but we're very excited and grateful to be here. It's going to be loads of fun," she said.

"I'm very excited about being on that stage and just performing and representing our country".

The song the pair will perform is Níos Láidre, the Irish word for stronger.

Caleb, who is 14 said the tune is "truly is about lifting people up and being there for one another and being very powerful on your own, but even more powerful with others".

Caleb, who has been training in the performing arts since the age of six said how proud he was of himself and Naomi for being able to represent Ireland.

"A few of my family and friends are coming over tonight and then a few tomorrow as well. And yeah, the support with our schools, our family, our friends, our performing arts schools, it's all just been amazing," he said.

"We're both so excited. We've already done a few rehearsals on the stage and everything's gone so well. So I think we're ready."

Caleb and Naomi's collaboration came during their individual searches to be Ireland's entry for the competition earlier this month.

The pair, who had entered individually were left standing at the end of the night with the judges unable to choose.

It was then decided they that both Caleb and Naomi would represent Ireland, together.

"It's very magical and we're just so happy being on the stage and it feels like our second home," said Naomi.

She added that the pair have had to opportunity to mingle with some of their competition from the other nations.

"We've gotten really close with Harry from Cyprus and we've gotten close with Eslin from Albania and Beppe from Malta and all of their dancers. And yeah, we've been having a lot of fun with all of the contestants. They're all really nice," Naomi said.

Caleb's mum Jennifer Kirwan, who has travelled to Malta alongside Naomi's mum has said the support "has been amazing".

"We've got family flying in at the moment. It's kind of getting very real, very exciting.

"It's lovely to have a few people here supporting us, but the outpour of support from friends, family, all their teams and schools, it's just been unbelievable. It's very, very special".

Support has exceeded just Ireland, Kirwan said the pair have "got people tuning in from our local families to Perth, to Brisbane, to America. We've gone global with the support, so it's brilliant."

Where can I watch Junior Eurovision 2026?

Fans have two windows to cast their votes. Unlike the main Eurovision contest, the public can vote for their own country.

Window one will open 22:59 BST on Friday until 19:59 on Saturday, just before the live show starts.

Voting will then reopen after the final song has been performed during the live show. There will be approximately 15 minutes to cast votes. All votes will be converted into points, which will be revealed during the show.

articles.title: This was a cost-saving way to travel the world. Then Covid changed everything
articles.summary: In our roundup of travel stories this week: the reality of living on a permanent cruise, the travelers visiting some of the world’s most notorious destinations, plus how the pandemic nearly killed off cargo ship tourism.
articles.body: In our roundup of travel stories this week: the reality of living on a permanent cruise, the travelers visiting some of the world’s most notorious destinations, plus how the pandemic nearly killed off cargo ship tourism. Cargo ship cruisers For centuries, cargo ships have welcomed paying passengers, making freighter tourism a niche but enduring industry. The golden age of voyages on board tramp steamers and banana boats was the first half of the 20th century. However, right up until the Covid pandemic, there were still half a dozen major players booking passengers on cargo ships going to remote ports of call. For aficionados, it’s a way to visit off-the-grid destinations untouched by mass tourism and to experience the romance and adventure of life onboard a working vessel. Most of the pre-pandemic operators are no longer in business. Covid-era health and safety issues put an end to many, combined with enhanced onboard security at a time when warfare and piracy are making the seas increasingly dangerous. Options may have dwindled, but there are still alluring cargo ship voyages on offer, to destinations such as Namibia, Iceland and French Polynesia. Companies such as Aranui and Neoliner Origin are even expanding their cargo-passenger services. Read more here to see where the seas might take you. New visa rules for Australia and Japan Australia has long been popular with backpackers and young people looking to see the world and pick up casual work. However, the government has announced a dramatic cut in the number of working holiday visas, from 31,000 to 5,000. To have a chance chance, visitors will have to pay hundreds of dollars to enter a lottery-style ballot. The government says it is about adjusting the intake to favor skilled migrants, who are seen to bring more value to the country’s economy. But not everyone is happy about it. Elsewhere in the Pacific, Japan has been experiencing a tourism boom, with record numbers arriving in recent years. The number of people settling down for longer-term stays, including work and study, also hit an all-time high last year. However, a series of tightened immigration policies imposed by the Japanese government has made some foreign residents wonder: Is it time to say “sayonara”? Life on a permanent cruise Here’s a selection of content for CNN subscribers. The residential cruise ship Villa Vie Odyssey launched in late 2024, after a bumpy start and no shortage of drama. By the time retired schoolteacher Sharon Lane joined the “forever” cruise in June 2025, however, most of the initial operational challenges had been ironed out and she was excited about a life permanently afloat. CNN caught up with her after her first year had passed to find out if reality matched expectations and how she and her fellow passengers were faring. There are even more unusual ways to explore the world than living on a cruise ship or traveling alongside cargo. Earlier this year, CNN talked to travelers choosing to vacation in war zones, radiation sites and volatile borderlands. The trend is known as “dark tourism” and it has two distinct strands: people visiting countries classed by other nations as dangerous, such as North Korea, Afghanistan and Haiti, and those going to places where notorious events happened, such as Jonestown in Guyana or Cambodia’s Killing Fields. Our streaming subscription service CNN All Access this week expanded internationally to Canada and the UK. In his CNN series “Parts Unknown,” Anthony Bourdain visited lesser-explored destinations around the world. Take a look at this episode from 2013, when he journeyed to Libya to see how the country was faring two years after the overthrow of Moammar Gadhafi. The world’s largest water village In case you missed it These are the 25 places National Geographic thinks you should visit in 2027. And why. A protest movement. A Washington makeover. A new iPhone era. What do you remember from the week that was? The diving vacation that went horribly wrong. A fun trip turned into a 13-hour fight for survival. “Cake sheds” are Britain’s new obsession. And they’re popping up everywhere.

articles.title: Gen Z are leading the European protests. Here’s why they’re angry
articles.summary: The kids are not alright. Across Europe, young people are protesting issues ranging from a lack of funding for education to the cost of housing, posing massive challenges to governments already under pressure and providing a visible sign of the intergenerational frustration felt by Gen Z.
articles.body: The kids are not alright. Across Europe, young people are protesting issues ranging from a lack of funding for education to the cost of housing, posing massive challenges to governments already under pressure and providing a visible sign of the intergenerational frustration felt by Gen Z. The precise configuration of these grievances varies from country to country. In Spain, the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from her home served as the catalyst for this wave of protests; in France, it was students demonstrating in support of striking teachers; student protests have rocked Albania on and off for months, first sparked by plans for a luxury development backed by US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner. Despite their different catalysts, however, all these movements have acted as a sort of black hole, drawing in any discontent before exploding in a catch-all outburst of frustration for a generation of young people who fear they won’t have the same opportunities as their parents. They have, in part, inspired each other, too. Protesters in Italy and Greece have referenced their French counterparts in their slogans. Housing protests in Spain spilled over into Portugal. And student unions across Europe are sharing advice and their experiences with one another, Alice de Brito, vice president of France’s main student union, UNEF, told CNN. “I see so many more similarities than differences,” she said. “We are all talking about the need for investments in education, in the universities, in youth in general. But we are also talking about the cost of living, about housing.” That echoes the demands made by Italian student union leader Sabrina Brizzola, who told a rally last weekend: “Let’s… make ourselves heard for schools that don’t collapse on our heads, for safe and dignified work, for public healthcare, for social justice.” For Julius Fintelmann, the co-founder and editor-in-chief of the European Correspondent daily newsletter, the protests “reflect a kind of frustration, the feeling that Europe’s politics is failing to deliver for the next generation.” As well as education and housing, he points to an increasingly uncertain job market, where artificial intelligence disproportionately affects entry-level jobs, and the climate crisis as laying the groundwork for this explosion of Gen Z anger. “I think fundamentally what we see is this promise that liberal democracy had, which was that the next generation will enjoy a better life than the current one, that promise simply doesn’t hold true anymore,” he told CNN. And the European Union countries most affected by protests – Greece, Italy, France, Belgium, Spain and Portugal – share a gloomy economic backdrop and high levels of national debt, making it hard to increase public spending. Bond yields in France, for example, ticked up to their highest levels since 2002 on Wednesday, exerting more pressure on government budgets. ‘Waiting for an answer’ Student protests like this have been held at the start of the French school year in September and October for the past nine years as young people returning to education realize they don’t have enough teachers or good equipment, noted de Brito. This year, however, they snowballed, as students demanded reduced class sizes, increased spending on teachers, investment in infrastructure to withstand the climate crisis and an end to police violence against young people. “People are just tired of waiting for an answer,” de Brito said. Education is a theme that cuts across Europe’s borders. Thousands of students and teachers marched across Greece, including a group who gathered outside parliament in Athens chanting, “from Greece to France, we want public, free education,” according to Reuters. When students first occupied a high school in Rome, on October 7, they wrote “like in France” in the first line of the statement defending their actions. The Italian government has sought to downplay any similarities with the protest movement in France. “The situation in Italy is very different from France,” Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara said earlier this month, repeating a far-right claim that the French protests are fueled by the difficulty, absent in Italy, of integrating second-generation migrants into the school system. Nonetheless, housing is another issue that cuts across national borders. Italian protesters say they have closely watched housing protests in Spain, which erupted in earnest in September and ultimately forced the government to call snap elections. Students at a protest camp in Rome told CNN that affordable housing was inseparable from a good education. One, Elisa Pastore, said she and her brother can “barely” afford the rent for their shared room in the Italian capital, where they attend university. For the first half of her degree, before her brother started university too, she had to commute 120 kilometers (75 miles) from outside Rome in order to save money. Other groups are protesting, too. A blockade by truckers in Italy, outraged by the rising cost of fuel following the Iran war, has halted production of buffalo mozzarella and some pasta. And issues like housing transcend generational divides, drawing older generations into the protests as well. In Portugal, thousands of people have gathered in Rossio Square, one of Lisbon’s busiest plazas, every evening this week. Some even pitched tents and 55 people were arrested in the early hours of Tuesday morning, prompting further demonstrations. Protesters, waving flags with slogans like “Casas para morar,” meaning “Homes to live in,” have demanded caps on rent hikes and the reversal of a new law that would make evictions easier. Elsewhere, long-running demonstrations in Albania and Serbia have focused more on anti-corruption, spiraling into movements seeking to topple each country’s government. After the protests in Albania turned violent last week, Prime Minister Edi Rama resisted any calls to step down, instead accusing protesters of threatening his plans for the country to join the EU and blaming his political opponents for the unrest. “We want a change, that’s why we’re here,” one protester in Albania told Reuters. “We want a revolution, we want a new government, we are not looking for any negotiations, we need a new government as soon as possible.” Meanwhile in Serbia, the student-led protests that have shaped the country’s politics for the past two years now form the most formidable opposition to longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in parliamentary elections on Sunday. More demonstrations are on the way. France is bracing for yet another wave of protests, with authorities racing to prevent a repeat of the kind of public disorder seen last weekend. A large demonstration is set to take place in Paris on Saturday afternoon, organized by France’s main student uion, UNEF, with one of the country’s biggest trade unions, CGT, announcing it will join. Other groups are expected to attend, including farmers, climate activists and the Yellow Vests, the movement that first emerged in 2018 during the protests over fuel costs. While the protest in Paris has been authorized by the authorities, French President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday banned all non-trade union protests on Saturday as he seeks to control the civil unrest. Nonetheless, widespread demonstrations are expected in Orléans, where hard-right figurehead Marine Le Pen launches her presidential campaign this weekend. Major trade unions in France and Spain have called for a general strike on November 5 and 11, respectively. In Germany, a group calling itself “Gen Z regelt” (“Gen Z’s got it”) has called for nationwide protests on October 31. And student unions in Britain and Italy are planning a day of action on November 20 to protest the rising cost of education.

articles.title: Guernsey visitor numbers arriving by air up by 12% this year
articles.summary: Half of people flying to Guernsey are now visitors, up from 42% two years ago.
articles.body:
The number of visitors arriving in Guernsey by air has increased by 12% in the first eight months of 2026, with first-time visitors up 30% compared with the same period in 2025.

According to Guernsey Ports air passengers spent £82.6 million, up £8.7 million on January to August 2025.

It said 238,953 individual passengers left Guernsey by air, in the first eight months of 2026 and half of them were visitors to the island.

There were 49,000 travellers from airports in London, including 16,000 on the Heathrow servcie which started in May.

Deputy Sasha Kazantseva-Miller, the president of the economic development committee, said the figures were "very encouraging for 2026, despite the geopolitical uncertainty and the changing travel patterns we are seeing".

She said it was "particularly positive" to see more people visit for the first time.

Alan Sillett, the president of the Guernsey Hospitality Association said accommodation suppliers had seen and increase in occupancy every month between January and August, apart from February.

The summer months had a 5% increase in room bookings and he said the trend carried on into Spetember.

"These are encouraging signs for the industry and reflect the importance of maintaining good air and sea connectivity, alongside continued efforts to attract visitors to Guernsey and encourage them to stay overnight," Sillett added.

articles.title: DNA project to restore black poplar trees across Thames Valley
articles.summary: Conservation groups say black poplars are endangered due to felling, land drainage and habitat loss.
articles.body:
A project is aiming to help restore one of the UK's rare native trees across the Thames Valley using DNA testing.

Conservation groups have warned numbers of black poplar trees have fallen due to decades of felling, land drainage and habitat loss.

The Swindon to Oxford: Regenerating the Thames and Tributaries nature recovery programme is working with local conservation groups to regenerate the population along the River Thames and its flood plain.

Catrina Bass, from the Long Mead Foundation in Swindon, is involved in the project and said while the trees were "extraordinary survivors", there were just 50 recorded in Oxfordshire currently.

Describing black poplars as "Lord of the Rings" looking trees with "great gnarled trunks", she said they support other wildlife, including the poplar hornet moth.

The project secured initial funding from West Oxfordshire District Council and the Vale of White Horse Council but is now aiming to raise £20,000 for the work, which involves DNA analysis of existing trees, propagating new cuttings and planting them in suitable sites.

Oxfordshire County Council's Local Nature Recovery Strategy has committed to match fund the fundraiser up to £10,000.

Also involved in the project is the Trust for Oxfordshire's Environment, which works with community groups to fund local environmental projects.

Chief executive Benjamin Heaven Taylor said black poplars play an important role in reducing flood risk, by lining rivers and floodplains, holding water back.

He said the population that remained was "extremely fragmented", adding that it "needs a helping hand to recover".

articles.title: Has Vivek Ramaswamy’s attack ad against Amy Acton backfired?
articles.summary: Ramaswamy’s ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother draws Republican criticism as Ohio governor’s race heats up.
articles.body:
An attack advertisement by Republican Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy targeting his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton, has sparked criticism within his own party, less than two weeks before November 3 midterm elections in the United States.

The ad features Acton’s estranged mother accusing Acton of being a liar.

Ramaswamy has refused to withdraw the ad, even as senior Republicans have called for its removal.

So what does the ad show, why has it sparked controversy and could it affect Ohio’s governor’s race?

The ad, which began circulating online on Monday, features Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, accusing her daughter of lying about her childhood and suggesting she has a mental illness.

“It’s not easy for a mother to say this, but Amy has a serious problem. She is a liar. She lies about her past,” Arthur said in the video.

Arthur also disputed Acton’s account of experiencing homelessness and living in a tent as a child as she urged Ohioans not to vote for her daughter.

However, the ad does not mention that the two have been estranged since 1978 when Acton was 12 and was removed from her mother’s custody after her stepfather was charged with raping her.

Her stepfather pleaded not guilty but failed to appear in court and was never tried. Acton and her brother have publicly described the abuse they experienced as children.

Court records and news reports from the time support key elements of Acton’s account of her childhood. FactCheck.org also found records linking her stepfather to the campground where Acton said her family lived in a tent, contradicting Arthur’s claim that the family never lived there.

Arthur remained married to Acton’s stepfather until his death.

On Tuesday, Ramaswamy’s campaign confirmed it was behind the advertisement and announced plans to spend $4m promoting it.

On Tuesday, Acton’s campaign released a statement recounting her childhood and a response ad featuring her brother, Phil Stearns.

“I received a lot of abuse, but Amy always got the worst of it,” Stearns said. “She continued to receive that abuse because she knew she had to protect me.”

The use of Acton’s family history has raised questions about how far political campaigns should go in attacking opponents.

David Niven, a political science professor at Ohio’s University of Cincinnati, told Al Jazeera that while campaigns have used relatives to criticise candidates before, this advertisement was particularly unusual.

“We’ve seen family members used before but not in such a deeply personal way,” Niven said.

“So we occasionally see a family member who’s talking about disagreements, you know, talking about a different kind of political outlook, but not this degree of just personal destruction. That’s what’s unprecedented here.”

How have Trump and other Republicans responded?

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance have defended Ramaswamy while other senior Republicans have called for the ad to be withdrawn.

On Thursday, Trump described the ad as “very powerful” and said he had encouraged Ramaswamy to continue running it. Vance told Republicans to “stop whining” about the controversy and focus on winning the elections.

Ohio Governor Mike DeWine, who has endorsed Ramaswamy, called the advertisement “deeply, deeply troubling” and urged its withdrawal although he maintained his endorsement.

Ohio Senator Jon Husted has also distanced himself from the ad.

Niven said the disagreement reflected a broader divide between traditional Republicans and the party’s Trump-aligned wing.

“So there’s a real divide between the Republican Party as it kind of traditionally was, that had something of a standard, and the Republican Party of Trump and Vance that will say anything at any time, regardless of the, you know, propriety of it.”

Ramaswamy has refused to withdraw the ad.

Vivek Ramaswamy , 41, is a Republican businessman and former biotechnology executive who unsuccessfully sought the party’s presidential nomination in 2024 before endorsing Trump.

Born and raised in Ohio, he is running for governor with the president’s endorsement.

Amy Acton, 60, is a physician and former director of the Ohio Department of Health who became nationally known for leading the state’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic under DeWine.

Raised in Youngstown, she has spoken publicly about experiencing poverty, homelessness and abuse during childhood.

Neither candidate has previously held elected office.

The ad could generate sympathy for Acton, particularly among survivors of sexual abuse and their families, according to political analysts.

“Every negative attack carries the risk of backfiring,” Jerry Miller, a professor of communication studies and a political advertising expert at Ohio University, told Al Jazeera.

He explained that campaigns sometimes use controversial advertisements to energise their supporters, even at the risk of alienating other voters.

“I do believe that this ad will generate a degree of empathy, particularly from sexual assault survivors and their families who have had to confront these issues,” he added.

Trump has survived numerous political controversies without losing the support of his base, but Niven said Ramaswamy may find it harder to move past this one.

“The thing that Trump has mastered is he’s always involved in a hundred controversies at a time,” he said. “So you kind of lose track of one controversy because it’s replaced by another one so quickly after.”

But Ramaswamy may not have that advantage.

“The problem for Ramaswamy is this is the only thing people are going to be seeing and hearing. He’s not going to be able to achieve the sort of Trump controversy distraction game,” Niven added.

Why does the controversy matter for Ohio’s governor’s race?

The controversy comes with Acton leading in several recent polls although some surveys suggested a closer contest.

On Friday, the Cook Political Report shifted the race from being a toss-up to leaning towards Acton. It cited the fallout from the advertisement. Its analysts said the race had already been moving towards Acton and the controversy had reinforced their assessment.

The backlash has also generated financial support for Acton, including a $500,000 donation from MK Pritzker, wife of Illinois Governor JB Pritzker.

Hundreds of Ohioans have already cast early ballots, and it remained unclear whether the controversy would influence undecided voters.

“What is already clear is that the controversy has taken on a life of its own, becoming a major factor in this campaign, independent of the ad that sparked it,” Miller told Al Jazeera.

Ohio is an important battleground in the November 3 elections . Once considered a swing state, it has voted for Trump in the past three presidential elections, and Republicans have held the governorship since 2011. A victory for Acton would make her the state’s first Democratic governor in 20 years.

articles.body: BERLIN — German police said they had detained a ​suspect after a fire broke out at ‌a historic mountain guest house known as the “Eagle’s Nest”, used as a retreat by Nazi ​officials, including the dictator Adolf ​Hitler. Around 200 firefighters and emergency personnel ⁠in the area around Berchtesgaden in ​the southern region of Bavaria were battling ​the flames after the building, known as the Kehlsteinhaus, caught fire on Friday, police said. Police ​are investigating whether the suspect, who ​was detained close to the scene, was connected to ‌the ⁠fire, they said in a statement. There was no immediate word about a possible motive. Built in 1938 as a guest ​house for ​Nazi ⁠officials and their guests, the building, in a spectacular Alpine ​setting, is separate from Hitler’s ​nearby ⁠summer residence, known as the Berghof. Now owned by the state of Bavaria, the ⁠Kehlsteinhaus ​was classified after the ​war as a historical monument recalling the Nazi period.

articles.title: FBI arrests Georgia man accused of throwing Molotov cocktail at Atlanta ICE facility
articles.summary: Inique Hinton faces up to 20 years after allegedly throwing a Molotov cocktail at the Atlanta ICE building in an act prosecutors called terrorism.
articles.body: Federal authorities arrested a 31-year-old Georgia man Thursday for allegedly throwing a Molotov cocktail at an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) building in downtown Atlanta earlier this week, in what prosecutors described as an "act of terrorism." Inique Hinton, of Douglasville, was charged with attempted arson of a federal building and depredation of government property, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Georgia. "An attack on federal property is an attack against our democracy. It is an act of terrorism. It is an act of political violence, and it cannot stand," U.S. Attorney Theodore Hertzberg said during a news conference. According to prosecutors, security cameras captured Hinton walking near the ICE building at 180 Ted Turner Drive just before 8:15 p.m. Tuesday. SUSPECT NAMED IN NEW YORK CITY ALLEGED INCENDIARY DEVICE ATTACK, HAD 'ANTI-ICE STUFF' ON HIM Minutes later, he allegedly ignited an object and threw it toward the facility, striking the exterior fence and causing flames to spread. Investigators said they recovered burned cloth, lighter fluid, a glass bottle and a lighter at the scene. Hinton was arrested Thursday by the FBI at a residence in Cobb County. "This was obviously an attack directed at the ICE facility," Hertzberg said, adding that prosecutors would respond with "extreme severity" because "we need to send the message that this is not OK." "We can talk about immigration, we can have civil discourse, but we cannot allow criminal acts, terroristic acts, like the one that was committed three days ago in our city," he continued. FBI INVESTIGATING AFTER ICE HEADQUARTERS IN PHOENIX RIDDLED WITH GUNFIRE Hertzberg also said the Atlanta ICE building had previously been targeted approximately six years earlier, during the summer of 2020. "I want to make very clear we are not going back to that," he said. "We will not tolerate attacks on government property and attacks against federal law enforcement." Atlanta police witnessed the incident and attempted to pursue the suspect but were unable to apprehend him that night. The FBI later released images of an unidentified suspect and offered a reward of up to $20,000 for information leading to his identification and arrest. Hinton faces a mandatory minimum of five years and a maximum of 20 years in federal prison if convicted of attempted arson, while the government-property charge carries a maximum penalty of 10 years. articles.body: CHHATRAPATI SAMBHAJINAGAR: A fancy “838” number plate, a daylight murder and screams of bystanders — horrific scenes unfolded on a busy road in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar on Thursday.A video of the incident shows the sequence of events as a man allegedly runs over his friend with a car before repeatedly bludgeoning him with a stick and an iron rod in broad daylight.The victim, Devesh alias Bunty Dixit (36), died on the spot, while the accused, Pawan Parashar (22), later drove to the Cidco police station and surrendered.How the chase ended in murderPreliminary investigation revealed that Dixit was returning home after a gym session when Parashar, a resident of Wankhedenagar, allegedly began pursuing him in a car.The chase ended near Mangesh Gas Agency in the N-7 area of Cidco. Police said Parashar rammed Dixit’s two-wheeler from behind, throwing him onto the road. The impact was so forceful that the two-wheeler was flung nearly 150 feet away.According to eyewitness accounts cited by police, Parashar then took a U-turn and drove back towards the injured man. He got out of the car and repeatedly struck Dixit on the head with a stick and an iron rod he had carried with him.“After the collision, the accused took a U-turn, drove back to the injured man, got out of the car and repeatedly attacked him on the head with a stick and an iron rod,” said Cidco inspector Atul Yerme.Dixit succumbed to his injuries at the spot before medical assistance could reach him.Accused surrenders at Cidco police stationThe killing triggered panic in the locality, with passersby and shopkeepers gathering at the scene. Senior police officers, including deputy commissioner of police (Zone II) Ratnakar Navale, visited the spot.Parashar subsequently drove to the Cidco police station and surrendered, police said.Friendship with victim allegedly turned into rivalryPolice suspect that a fallout between the two men led to the killing.“The accused, after surrendering before the police, claimed that he and the victim used to work as bouncers for different bars. He was upset due to their friendship turning into a rivalry,” Navale told TOI.He said police teams were cross-verifying the accused’s version and probing the exact motive behind the murder.Inspector (Crime) Gajanan Kalyankar said investigators were questioning Parashar to establish the complete sequence of events and ascertain the circumstances that led to the killing.Stay updated with the latest Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar news. articles.title: North Korea’s Kim Jong Un visits China via newly opened bridge
articles.summary: South Korean officials say Kim arrived in Dandong using the New Yalu River Bridge, which opened about a week ago.
articles.body:
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong via a newly opened bridge, according to South Korean officials.

The visit on Saturday comes about a week after the bridge linking the two countries was officially opened, 12 years after its completion, deepening economic ties between the Asian giant and its small, nuclear-armed neighbour.

Kim’s visit also comes a day before the anniversary of China joining the 1950–1953 Korean War.

Chinese Premier Li Qiang met Kim in the border city, the Reuters news agency said, quoting a South Korean official.

China’s foreign ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Kim arrived in Dandong through the New Yalu River Bridge connecting the two countries, the Reuters and AFP news agencies reported, quoting unnamed South Korean government officials. South Korea’s Yonhap News Agency also reported the visit, citing an unidentified government source.

Analysts say the visit represents part of Kim’s increasingly assertive foreign policy, as he seeks to align Pyongyang with Beijing and Moscow in a united front against the United States under what he portrays as a “new Cold War”.

Experts said the opening of the New Yalu River Bridge, which stretches 3km (1.9 miles) across the Yalu River, was a key symbol of strengthening ties between the two countries and reflected their intent to expand trade. It is expected to accommodate two-way traffic around the clock, including container shipments and heavy cargo trucks.

The four-lane structure was completed in 2014, but its opening was delayed due to a lack of connecting roads and customs facilities on the North Korean side, according to South Korean news reports.

“The opening of the bridge has resolved a major bottleneck in China-North Korea trade logistics,” Lu Chao, an expert in China-North Korea relations at the Liaoning Academy of Social Sciences, a Chinese government think tank in Shenyang, told Reuters.

“With the logistics constraint eased, bilateral trade is likely to increase further,” Lu said.

China is North Korea’s largest trading partner and a vital source of diplomatic, economic and political support for the reclusive state, although ties have not always been smooth.

China, which fought alongside North Korea in the Korean War, is Pyongyang’s main economic and diplomatic backer. However, North Korea has drawn closer to Russia since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which analysts say has reduced Pyongyang’s reliance on Beijing.

Kim’s last known visit to China was in September 2025 to attend the 80th Victory Day celebrations in Beijing, where he held a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Xi made a state visit to North Korea in June in which he expressed Beijing’s willingness to expand bilateral cooperation in trade, agriculture, construction and technology, while Kim described ties with China as a top strategic priority.

articles.title: In 2012, Josh Hutcherson bought a Hollywood Hills hideaway once owned by Heath Ledger for $2.5 million; eight years later, the 1951 home with a 2,500-square-foot deck sold for $2.94 million
articles.summary: Some homes boast standout features; others have stories etched into their walls. Josh Hutcherson’s former Hollywood Hills hideaway had both.
articles.body: Some homes boast standout features; others have stories etched into their walls. Josh Hutcherson’s former Hollywood Hills hideaway had both. Built in 1951, the secluded Midcentury Modern home is a perfect retreat and has a few famous names in its history. Tucked behind heavy landscaping, this secluded home has had several famous owners, from Ellen DeGeneres and Heath Ledger to Josh Hutcherson himself. Josh Hutcherson bought the half-acre, wood-clad Hollywood gem in 2012 for $2.94 million. In 2019, he sold the home for $2.94 million, the Los Angeles Times reports.A home with famous ownersThe house sits behind thick landscaping, so most people driving past never see it. That’s one of the reasons why famous people have consistently sought it out. The Hunger Games actor Josh Hutcherson bought the property through a trust in 2012, according to public records. He was not the first well-known name on the deed. Talk-show host Ellen DeGeneres bought the house for $1.3 million and later sold it to actor Heath Ledger for $2.3 million, the Daily Mail reported. After Ledger’s death, his estate sold the home for $2.5 million. Furniture designer Guy Chaddock also lived in the secluded Hollywood Hills home at some point.Inside the retreat-like homeThe Midcentury Modern home spans nearly 1,900 square feet, with two bedrooms and two bathrooms, People reported. Polished concrete floors run through the home, and beamed ceilings sit overhead. A fireplace and brick wall fill the far end of the living room. Glass doors open from that room onto the outdoor deck.The kitchen has been updated with modern stainless-steel Miele and Sub-Zero appliances, plus a wine fridge. A small office and reading nook sit just off the kitchen area. The layout is simple, and that seems to be the point. The house was built for quiet days and easy movement between the rooms and the outdoors.The deckThe outdoor area is where the home really stretches out. The deck adds about 2,500 square feet of living space, according to the listing. It includes a sunken conversation pit and a lounge area with a drop-down projector. The space also has an outdoor grill and a screening room.The deck looks over a private, wooded hillside. No wonder the home is often called a ‘tree house’. For a property of this size, that view does a lot of the selling!The home was listed for about $3.5 million, according to the Daily Mail. It sold for $2.94 million, a figure close to what Hutcherson paid eight years earlier. The sale brought the property’s price history full circle, at least in terms of what he got back.Deedee Howard and Charlie Heydt of The Agency were the listing agents. Paul Salazar of Hilton & Hyland represented the buyer.For the buyer, the house offers a perfect retreat and privacy. Its 1951 bones remain intact, with original features such as the beamed ceilings and fireplace wall. The updated kitchen and appliances make it easier to live in day to day. The property also carries the names of its previous famous owners. Each owner has added a chapter to its story, and the next buyer will inherit that history along with the wood, concrete and glass!Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Amir Shokeen remanded in 5-day police custody by Delhi court in viral video case involving racial abuse of Tripura youth
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Content creator Amir Shokeen was remanded in five days of police custody by a Delhi court on Saturday in connection with a viral video
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Content creator Amir Shokeen was remanded in five days of police custody by a Delhi court on Saturday in connection with a viral video allegedly showing a youth from Tripura being subjected to racial abuse and humiliation.Police told the court that Shokeen needs to be taken to Ahmedabad to identify and arrest other people suspected of being involved in the incident.Shokeen was produced before Additional Sessions Judge Shilpi Jain after his one-day judicial custody, granted on Friday, ended.Amir Shokeen arrested in viral video case Delhi Police arrested Shokeen on Thursday after taking suo motu cognisance of the video circulating on social media. The footage allegedly showed a youth from Tripura being subjected to racial remarks and humiliation.The case is being investigated by the Intelligence Fusion and Strategic Operations (IFSO) unit of Delhi Police following a communication from the Special Police Unit for North Eastern Region (SPUNER).According to police sources, the video was allegedly recorded in Ahmedabad around a month ago. Investigators are examining the roles of seven to eight people in connection with the incident. Kiren Rijiju, Tripura CM Manik Saha condemn racial abuseThe incident drew widespread condemnation, with Union Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju and Tripura Chief Minister Manik Saha calling for action against those involved.Saha had directed the Tripura director general of police to coordinate with Delhi Police in the matter. Rijiju, meanwhile, said the accused would face strict action.Tripura Students Forum seeks impartial probeThe Tripura Students Forum Delhi also called for an impartial investigation into the incident. It sought the preservation of electronic evidence, including the original video recording, metadata, account details and upload history.The investigation is continuing as police seek to establish the roles of others allegedly involved in the incident.(With agency inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news.
