articles.title: How reliant is Ukraine on US support – and could Kyiv carry on without it?
articles.summary: It has been a bewildering week in US-Ukraine relations. Amid continuing tensions, experts say there are three broad levers of pressure the US can apply to Kyiv.
articles.body: It has been a bewildering period in US-Ukraine relations, after US President Donald Trump slammed his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky for failing to negotiate an end to the war and Kyiv accused Washington of withholding key military support. Trump then sent his envoy to Norway and Russia to try to advance the peace process – but Washington walked away with only a plan to resume trilateral talks. Meanwhile, deadly Russian attacks continue, as Ukraine raises concerns about cracks in support from the US. The latest tensions are far from the first bout between Kyiv and Trump, who began his second term by halting aid for Ukraine’s war effort. Since then, Europe has picked up the tab and Kyiv has built up its own defense industry at a rapid pace. So how much does Ukraine still rely on US support? And can it carry on fighting without it? Experts say there are three broad levers of pressure the United States can apply to Kyiv – economic, military and political – as it seeks some sort of Ukrainian capitulation to end the war started by Russia. Economic: Ukraine aid already cut The Trump administration halted new aid packages for Ukraine at the beginning of 2025. Before then, the US had sent at least $131.5 billion in total aid to Ukraine, which still makes it the largest single donor since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, according to data from the Kiel Institute for the World Economy, a German think tank that tracks wartime aid to Ukraine. Some of the weapons from American manufacturers purchased during the Biden administration are still flowing to Ukraine, but many of those contracts have been fulfilled. European Union countries and institutions as a bloc now outpace the US in their total donations, sending at least $228.5 billion since 2022, Kiel Institute data shows. Germany, Denmark, the Netherlands and Sweden have given the largest amount of military aid among the EU states. The United Kingdom and Norway have also contributed a significant chunk of military aid from outside the bloc. Many of the donations come in the form of NATO allies purchasing US-made weapons that they then transfer to Ukraine. But those European weapons transfers still require Pentagon authorization, giving the Trump administration another source of leverage. Zelensky addressed Ukraine’s critical shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors on Friday, saying, “The delivery of interceptors to protect us against Russian ballistic missiles is still delayed. We are waiting for interceptors that were already agreed on, but they are still not coming.” Last week, Ukraine ran out of Patriot interceptors – one of the few defensive weapons capable of knocking down a ballistic missile – leaving it far more vulnerable to Russian attacks. None of the ballistic missiles that slammed Kyiv overnight into Thursday were intercepted – an indicator that Patriot stocks are still empty or critically low. Zelensky told CNN hours after that attack that Ukraine primarily needs two things from its allies at this critical moment: “Not to lift sanctions from Putin … (and) to give us better missiles.” Given that those weapons orders are a boon for American defense companies, analysts say it’s unlikely that any slow-down or blocking of purchases would continue for a long time. Military: Intel sharing and satellite internet Although American financial support has collapsed, Ukraine still relies heavily on US intelligence and technology. It has no replacement for unique American systems like the Patriot interceptors, the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite internet called Starshield and advanced missile-warning technology. “That is something Europeans don’t have, and they don’t have it because we (the US) have told them for the last 30 years not to develop it … because they can rely on us,” said Max Bergmann, the Russia program director at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a Washington-based think tank. “We’re in a situation where America is proving to everyone in Europe that it simply can’t be relied upon,” Bergmann told CNN. “This could be really devastating for Ukraine in the sense that it could cause tremendous economic damage, tremendous loss of civilian life, civilians leaving,” he said. “But I doubt it’s going to actually break Ukraine’s will to fight.” Zelensky said earlier this week that on multiple occasions Ukraine had received no US intelligence warnings of ballistic strikes. That resulted in Russian missile attacks hitting without the usual air raid sirens warning residents to head to bunkers, and Ukrainian officials have said more civilians died as a result. The US State Department and Trump himself have denied limiting intelligence sharing. By Tuesday night, Zelensky said that the intelligence sharing with the United States “now works” again. The country’s defense ministry said Saturday full access to Starshield has been restored though it was not immediately clear if the restoration of Starshield speeds could be felt across the country. One source on the ground in Ukraine’s Donetsk region told CNN Saturday morning that the speed in their area continued to be limited to 160 kilometers per hour. The restrictions, which disrupt any military ordnance moving at high speeds, have hindered Ukrainian interceptor drones in defending against Russian attacks and upended Ukrainian military operations in many areas of the front line, Ukrainian officials said. Trump and some of his top officials have denied making the call to throttle Ukraine’s use of the Starshield service, without offering any clear explanation for what had actually happened. Earlier this week, Trump said he was not involved. Musk has denied taking unilateral action, though, saying in a social media post that “any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.” In the short term, any further disruptions or restrictions to US-backed systems are likely to hit Ukraine incredibly hard, experts said. In the long-term, it’s likely that European allies will pump more money into developing their own systems to help Ukraine. “I think the Ukrainians probably didn’t think that the United States would stoop this low, would betray it this much, because this isn’t really an act of charity that the United States is doing. … This is a service that Ukraine is spending money on,” Bergmann said of Kyiv’s Starshield contract and Patriot interceptor purchases. “What the administration is doing actually has far larger ramifications for the basic reliability of the US as a technology and defense supplier,” Bergmann added. Political: Giving hope to Putin The falling-out between the US and Ukraine also has wider geopolitical ramifications, analysts said, and could end up being a gift to the Kremlin’s war effort. It comes after a number of controversial moves by the Trump administration this month, including waiving new sanctions on Russia before they could kick in and striking a deal to allow Russia to export diesel. Meanwhile, the Kremlin has so far not budged on its maximalist demands to end the war. Washington’s willingness to place unprecedented pressure on Kyiv “gives Russia a certain hope that if they continue fighting this war, eventually the European resolve will also fade away,” said Natia Seskuria, a senior research fellow on Russia and Eurasia at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK-based defense think tank. John Lough, head of international partnerships at the New Eurasian Strategies Centre, had a similar view. “I think the Russians must feel quite pleased with themselves at the moment with the strain all this recent activity is putting on Europe, by getting Trump to pressurize Ukraine, break the sanctions regime and not follow through with the Lindsey Graham bill,” he told CNN. “It’s just accentuating the fact that Europe and the United States are not aligned.” Trump has directly tied the waiving of sanctions to the release of detained American Stephen Hubbard, despite stating earlier that the US gave Moscow “nothing in exchange” for his freedom. Experts said some of the tension – particularly on issues related to diesel, with Trump blaming Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for soaring prices rather than the Iran war – may dissipate after the US midterms. But the problem of high gas prices and the unpopularity of the Iran war are here to stay for the remainder of Trump’s presidency, Lough argued. Lough said that Ukraine’s efforts to continue attacks on Russian oil refineries have been like “a red rag to a bull” for Trump. “It makes Ukraine the easy target if you’re trying to deflect responsibility for what’s happened with Iran.” CNN’s Becky Pinnington contributed to this report.

articles.title: Megan Thee Stallion’s foundation helped Mila launch a mental health project with a $550 grant; after starting in 2024, her nonprofit reports delivering more than 2,200 care packages to Black girls
articles.summary: A $550 grant helped a 12-year-old girl turn her own mental health struggles into a project that has since reached thousands of others.
articles.body: A $550 grant helped a 12-year-old girl turn her own mental health struggles into a project that has since reached thousands of others. Mila Henry launched MH Boxes in January 2024 after receiving a microgrant through the #BlackGirlJoyChallenge, an initiative backed by rapper Megan Thee Stallion’s Pete & Thomas Foundation and the Southern Black Girls & Women’s Consortium. What began as a small effort to support Black girls facing mental health challenges has grown into a nonprofit that now reports delivering 3,303 care packages across 17 states and Washington, DC, according to its official website.The boxes contain journals, fidget toys, affirmations and other self-care tools designed to help Black girls feel supported and encourage conversations about mental health. The project draws on Mila’s own experiences and her belief that young people facing emotional difficulties should have access to resources that recognise their needs and make them feel less alone. The initiative also highlights how relatively small grants can help young people turn personal experiences into community-led projects.How a personal struggle inspired MH BoxesMila came up with the idea after experiencing anxiety and receiving mental health treatment herself. In a May 2024 profile, Richmond Family Magazine reported that she had struggled with anxiety and depression during middle school and had been hospitalised for mental health treatment towards the end of the Covid-19 pandemic. Her experience helped her recognise that other girls might also need encouragement and practical resources when dealing with emotional difficulties.The care packages were designed specifically for Black girls, who Mila and her family believed were not always adequately represented in conversations about mental health. The boxes include tactile items such as slime, modelling clay and fidget toys, alongside journals, handmade bracelets, positive messages and information about mental health resources. The aim is not to replace professional treatment, but to offer reassurance and tools that can make it easier for girls to acknowledge their feelings and seek support.Mila initially distributed the boxes through educators, mental health providers, schools and community organisations in central Virginia. By May 2024, Richmond Family Magazine reported that she had delivered more than 500 packages.The $550 grant that helped turn the idea into a nonprofitThe project received an early boost through the #BlackGirlJoyChallenge, a collaboration between the Pete & Thomas Foundation and the Southern Black Girls & Women’s Consortium. The initiative was created to help young Black women develop community projects focused on mental health, wellness and spreading joy. In its 2024 edition, 100 young women received $550 microgrants to put their ideas into action.Mila used her grant to establish MH Boxes in January 2024. The project subsequently developed into a nonprofit organisation focused on providing culturally affirming mental health support to Black girls. The Pete & Thomas Foundation was established in 2022 in honour of Megan Thee Stallion’s late parents. Its work includes supporting initiatives involving education, housing and health and wellness in underserved communities.The grant programme illustrates how funding can help young people move beyond an idea and establish projects that respond to needs they have experienced themselves.From 500 packages to more than 3,300MH Boxes has continued expanding since its launch. In July 2025, Axios reported that Mila had distributed 1,600 boxes across five states. The report also noted that Megan Thee Stallion praised Mila’s work when the teenager received the Pete & Thomas Foundation’s Young Humanitarian Award at an event in New York.The nonprofit’s website now lists 3,303 mental health boxes delivered to Black girls across 17 states and Washington, DC. Its impact page had previously reported that more than 2,200 packages had reached girls during the organisation’s first year.The figures indicate the project's reported growth from a local effort into a wider initiative. The packages reach girls through schools, community partners and families, helping extend the project beyond its original distribution network.MH Boxes also says its work is expanding beyond the physical packages. Its broader vision includes youth leadership, advocacy, peer support and efforts to help Black girls participate in decisions affecting their mental health.Why representation matters in mental health supportThe organisation says its work is intended to address stigma and barriers that can prevent Black girls from accessing or discussing mental health support. Its packages are designed with their intended recipients in mind, combining practical items with messages that affirm their worth and encourage them to talk about difficult feelings. By including information about mental health resources, the initiative also aims to help girls and families identify additional avenues of support.The need for such resources extends beyond the boxes themselves. Mental health care can involve professional counselling, treatment and support from families, schools and communities. MH Boxes positions its packages as one part of that wider network rather than a substitute for clinical care.The organisation's next phase includes building youth leadership opportunities and developing programmes intended to help Black girls influence mental health policy and access pathways into mental health careers.You use AI every day. articles.title: Rubio calls on Cubans to partner with CIA ‘to create positive change’
articles.summary: Washington has raised pressure on Havana after the capture of former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.
articles.body:
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has called on those seeking change in Cuba to partner with the CIA and help force an end to the island’s communist government.

US President Donald Trump and other senior US officials have for months openly hinted at military intervention and permanent presence in Cuba to ramp up economic, political, and legal pressure on the country.

On Friday, Rubio seemed to openly confirm this when he wrote on X: “To those who seek to create positive change in Cuba – now is the time.”

Rubio commented on “the disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few” in Cuba, encouraging civilians to “seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discreet partnership with the CIA”.

The call was mocked by Cuban officials, including Deputy Foreign Minister Carlos Fernandez de Cossio.

“Now the United States is resorting to public recruitment for the CIA… There must be a great deal of desperation or misery within the agency for it to be forced to sell its services like a tube of toothpaste,” he wrote on X.

This is far from the first time Cuba has been threatened with military intervention by US officials.

Last month, Fernandez de Cossio told the US cable television channel C-SPAN’s flagship programme, Washington Journal, that it would be an “ atrocious international crime for the US to use military force against Cuba, which is a peaceful neighbouring country”.

The CIA later uploaded a video on X offering instructions in Spanish for those who believe they have information of interest to the intelligence agency, encouraging them to first and foremost visit an official “US embassy in person” if they can safely travel to one.

These latest developments come as a US-imposed oil blockade on Cuba earlier this year has put civilians in the country under intense economic hardship , as they contend with fuel shortages and blackouts exacerbated by failing infrastructure.

United Nations rights experts have condemned the oil blockade as ‌a violation of international law, while rights advocates say the Trump administration’s threats have echoed an imperialist approach.

Washington has maintained an embargo on Cuba for ⁠more than 60 years, as the Trump administration steps up pressure on Havana following the US military’s capture of Venezuelan then-President Nicolas Maduro in a deadly ⁠raid in January.

articles.title: The Muslims finding belonging in southern Spain
articles.summary: Centuries after the end of Islamic rule, some Muslims are choosing Andalusia, drawn by traces of its past.
articles.body:
Alora, Spain - The train chugs steadily out of Malaga station, its rhythmic clatter carrying it inland towards the mountains of the Guadalhorce Valley, where whitewashed villages cling to hillsides.

Beyond the window, pomegranate trees grow close to the tracks. Palms and cypress trees stand alongside young orange saplings planted in neat rows and, farther out, olive groves whose leaves shimmer between green and silver in the breeze. Above the rugged mountains, small white clouds float across an immense blue sky, like pieces of popcorn.

Over the train's rattle, an announcement in Spanish comes through the speakers: “The next station is Aljaima.”

The name derives from the Arabic al-khaima , meaning “the tent”, a small echo of another language, another time.

And then Alora, where the town rises around a rocky hill crowned by the remains of an old fortress. Some etymologists suggest the town's ancient name may derive from the Arabic a l-lawra , loosely translated as "the light".

The railway station is quiet in the midday heat.

A large black pick-up truck rumbles into the station car park and stops. Henrietta Szovati, a British-Hungarian Muslim, steps out, having driven down from the mountains to collect provisions.

Dressed in a loose blue shirt and cream trousers, she offers a warm embrace. Silver earrings dangle beside her face, and a sea-blue scarf is wrapped around her hair like a turban. A pair of red-framed spectacles rests on top.

She apologises for the truck’s state. Dust has settled on the dashboard, and bits of dried grass have found their way inside. “It is a working vehicle,” she says, more accustomed to hauling things across farmland than ferrying visitors from railway stations.

For the past two years, she and her husband, Ajmal Masroor, a therapist and imam, have been transforming an old farmhouse and its surrounding land into the House of Andalus. The project aims to bring people closer to southern Spain's Islamic history and the natural world.

Nearly 400 olive trees dot the 14 hectares (35 acres). She wants to plant more and make it a thousand-tree olive grove, she says with a smile, glancing out of the truck's open window.

The road winds higher into the mountains. Wildfires, Henrietta says, swept through parts of the surrounding region at the height of summer, and the landscape still bears the season's harshness. Reddish-brown earth gives way to patches of parched scrub and exposed rock, while slabs of silvery-grey stone jut sharply from the slopes.

"That's slate," Henrietta explains, pointing through the windscreen. The Spanish word is pizarra , she adds, the same name as the neighbouring town.

Oranges flourish here, as do figs and avocados. And mangoes that are better than those from South Asia, Henrietta emphatically declares.

As we drive further into the mountains, Henrietta gestures towards a neighbouring property. “That's my neighbour, Juan Garcia.”

Henrietta buys lemons, avocados and honey from him. Sometimes he comes over to help with the olives. It's this sense of community and neighbourliness she found harder to come by in Britain, where she has lived since 2001, marrying Ajmal a year later.

"I feel like an outsider there. I'm still not ‘one of us’ after more than 20 years."

As a Muslim and as a European, she says, Spain feels familiar in a way no other place does. Hungary was never an option, she adds, describing its government as “racist and right-wing”. And in Britain, she says, being Muslim can feel unavoidably political, her faith viewed through headlines and public arguments about Islam.

In the mountains above Alora, she feels her neighbours meet her first as Henrietta: the woman who lives up the track and joins in village life.

"Practising Islam here is just easier," she adds.

Yet Spain is not immune to the political currents sweeping across Europe. The far-right Vox party has made opposition to immigration and what it calls the "Islamisation" of Spain central to its campaigning, raising questions about how secure that sense of belonging might be.

With a sigh, Henrietta acknowledges that being Muslim can be difficult anywhere in the world today. But she prefers to focus on what she can build, rather than on political circumstances beyond her control. "Circumstances change, but community, connections and faith don’t," she says.

For her, that means building relationships with neighbours, even when they hold different beliefs. A sense of community, she argues, is forged through everyday encounters rather than political rhetoric.

On a visit to Juan Garcia’s home, his 79-year-old mother, Maria, is curious about the scarf wrapped around Henrietta's hair.

The women are standing in Maria's living room, its shutters drawn against the afternoon sun. A portrait of Jesus hangs on the wall.

Henrietta explains that she is Muslim and that covering her hair is part of her faith, a way to feel closer to God. Maria is Catholic. The conversation turns to the Virgin Mary, who also covered her hair.

But Maria insists all that matters is being a good person. If you cannot be good, none of the outward signs of faith means very much.

There is no awkwardness between them, no need to defend or explain their beliefs. The conversation moves on.

It is such ordinary encounters that have made Andalucia feel like home, Henrietta says. But her connection to this part of Spain runs deeper than the friendships she is making. It also stems from a deep respect for a history that stretches back more than 1,000 years.

For British Muslim travel writer and historian Tharik Hussain, author of Muslim Europe, the fascination is understandable. Al-Andalus was the medieval Muslim-ruled territory of modern-day Spain and Portugal. Its heartland lay in the south, in what is now Andalucia, home to cities such as Cordoba, Seville and Granada, where surviving monuments still evoke a period when Muslims helped shape European civilisation.

Its eventual loss, he says, has given it an almost “Atlantis-like aura” in the Muslim imagination, a longing reflected in Muslim literature over the centuries, from the 17th-century historian al-Maqqari to the 20th-century poet Allama Iqbal.

For nearly eight centuries, Muslim dynasties ruled parts of the Iberian Peninsula, leaving behind palaces and fortresses with horseshoe arches, intricate zellij tilework, carved yeseria plasterwork, and curling Arabic calligraphy. Their legacy endured in irrigation channels known as acequias (from the Arabic al-saqiya ), scholarship, language and traditions that continued to shape Spain long after the fall of Granada in 1492.

Britons have long headed to Andalucia in search of a place in the sun. But among those putting down roots here are Muslims drawn by something more: The chance to reconnect with a history in which Islam was part of Europe, and to build lives where their faith feels less like a defining difference.

Yet the Andalucia they are entering is not a vanished kingdom waiting to be rediscovered; it is modern Spain, with its own economic pressures, social divisions, and complicated relationship with the past.

What happens when the dream of al-Andalus meets the realities of living here?

articles.title: Why is Israel launching a new military operation in the occupied West Bank?
articles.summary: Netanyahu says ‘we will destroy this place’ as Israeli forces begin days-long operation with raids and demolitions.
articles.body:
Israel’s military has launched another major operation in the occupied West Bank, during which it plans to carry out mass arrests, demolish homes and forcibly displace residents.

The operation comes after an attack at an Israeli military checkpoint near Hebron on Friday in which two Israeli soldiers were killed. The two suspected Palestinian gunmen were shot dead.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who ordered a full lockdown of the West Bank, said Israeli forces would go house-to-house in the Hebron neighbourhood that the suspected attackers came from.

“We will act to destroy this place, ⁠to change it completely,” he said.

Israeli rights group B’Tselem warned the Israeli government’s planned offensive amounts to “collective punishment and acts that could constitute war crimes”.

Here’s what we know about the Israeli military operation.

Israel’s military announced late on Friday that a major “counterterrorism” operation, involving Israeli soldiers, police and other security agents, was under way in the Hebron area of the occupied West Bank.

It said the “targeted” campaign would last “several days”, in addition to operations in “dozens” of other areas across the West Bank.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu earlier said Israeli forces would go “house-to-house” in the Hebron neighbourhood where the suspects involved in Friday’s attack came from, replicating tactics previously used in refugee camps in the northern West Bank . The operation will involve demolitions and forced displacement, he said.

By Saturday morning, Israeli forces had raided at least 15 towns in the northern West Bank, including Nablus, Jenin, Tubas and Qalqilya, arresting dozens of Palestinians, Al Jazeera correspondents reported.

On Saturday, videos posted on Telegram by Palestinians in the al-Jalda area of Hebron city showed Israeli soldiers standing guard and military vehicles, shopping trolleys and other objects blocking the roads.

Israeli forces in the area had also sent in a bulldozer that could be seen alongside other Israeli military vehicles.

Earlier, Israeli bulldozers wrecked a three-storey building in Hebron, while ordering hundreds of Palestinian families to leave their homes in the Ein Deir Bahha area of the city and its surroundings.

Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Ramallah in the West Bank, said there was “a lot of anxiety” in the occupied territory as people largely avoided going into the streets.

“Hebron is sealed off; seven district entrances are closed,” Odeh reported on Saturday. “Only one or two may allow some pedestrian traffic at times, and it’s extremely unpredictable.

“The Hebron municipality has told us that up to half of the neighbourhood attacked overnight by Israeli soldiers in Hebron has been forcibly displaced. At least 200 families are now forced to be outside their homes.”

Why has Israel locked down the West Bank?

The measure is a response to Friday’s attack at an Israeli checkpoint near Hebron.

But it also takes place just days before Israel’s election on Tuesday , during which Israel had already been planning to lock down the occupied territory, reported The Times of Israel.

During the lockdown, Netanyahu said Israeli troops would conduct “extensive waves of arrests” and pursue Hamas fighters “wherever they are and at all times”.

The operation comes amid signs that Israel and its ally the United States are preparing for a potential new wave of attacks on Iran.

According to The New York Times, the US and Israel have drafted plans for a campaign of attacks on Iran that would take place after the US midterm elections on November 3.

Citing unnamed US officials and other informed sources, The New York Times reported that the US and Israel have intensified drills for a “a short but intensive operation” against Iran, with potential targets to include the country’s “energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenal”.

US President Donald Trump appeared to confirm on Friday that the US was weighing a new military campaign against Iran. Speaking at a rally, Trump said, “We may do another little epic fury,” using the codename of the US-Israel war against Iran that started with attacks across the country on February 28.

How have attacks on Palestinians escalated?

Since the beginning of 2025, more than 40,000 citizens have been forcibly displaced from their homes by Israeli settler violence and raids by armed forces in the West Bank, and displacement continues to this day, The Palestinian Authority said in a statement on Saturday.

It warned of the dangers posed by the ongoing Israeli operation in Hebron, “where collective punishment measures include the forced displacement of entire neighbourhoods, the demolition of homes and structures, and the closure and siege of Palestinian cities”.

Israeli settler pogroms against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank have been particularly rife in recent weeks , coinciding with the annual olive harvest season.

On Saturday morning, Israeli settlers stormed the villages of Yabrud and Al Mughayyir, east of Ramallah, to forcibly graze their sheep on the agricultural lands of Palestinians and damage their crops, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.

On Thursday, the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission said it had recorded 409 attacks by Israeli forces or settlers against Palestinian farmers, their land, olive trees and agricultural equipment so far during October. It called the attacks part of a pattern of “direct violence to force farmers from their land”.

Visiting Western officials have also found themselves caught up in the violence.

On October 17, Israeli settlers assaulted European diplomats, including a French mayor, near the Palestinian village of Taybeh in the occupied West Bank as they visited Palestinian olive farmers. Then on Wednesday, US Democratic congressional candidate Brad Lander was briefly detained by the Israeli military while volunteering to help Palestinian farmers harvest olives.

What has the response been to Israel’s West Bank operation?

The operation has been cheered on by far-right Israeli officials, but criticised by the United Nations and human rights watchdogs.

Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who also holds a position within Israel’s Ministry of Defence where he oversees the administration of the occupied West Bank and its settlements, called for Israel’s large-scale offensive in the West Bank to proceed “exactly like in Gaza”.

Israel’s National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir called for the Ramallah-based Palestinian Authority to be “dismantled” and for tighter restrictions on Palestinian movement.

Mustafa Barghouti, secretary-general of the Palestinian National Initiative party, said incitement from far-right Israeli ministers was making the situation worse.

He told Al Jazeera the West Bank lockdown was turning every city and village into “a small prison”, a form of collective punishment that would “lead to explosions”.

Mayy El Sheikh, spokesperson for the UN’s Human Rights Office in the occupied Palestinian territory, said Israel’s move to lock down the West Bank marked “yet another episode in a never-ending stream of suffocating measures making life more and more unbearable for Palestinians”.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, through his spokesperson, also expressed concern about West Bank closures that would restrict Palestinians’ “access to basic services and livelihoods”.

B’Tselem sounded the alarm over Israeli “plans for collective punishment and acts that could constitute war crimes”.

“The world cannot stand by as Israel continues its assault on Palestinians, waiting for yet more neighbourhoods to be emptied and erased before intervening, despite what we have already witnessed in Gaza and the northern West Bank,” said the rights group.

articles.title: In 2020, Ashley Benson bought a 1930 Los Angeles mansion for $4.5 million, removed walls and added a speakeasy; three years later, the restored property sold for $8.5 million, $4 million above her purchase price
articles.summary: For three years, Ashley Benson poured time and effort into making her Los Feliz house her own. And then she sold it.
articles.body: For three years, Ashley Benson poured time and effort into making her Los Feliz house her own. And then she sold it. Now, the carefully curated home belongs to someone else. In 2020, the Pretty Little Liars alum bought the 1930 Spanish Revival home in Laughlin Park, a guard-gated community in Los Feliz, for $4.5 million, and then sold it in 2023 for $8.5 million. The asking price was $9.5 million, according to Robb Report, and yet $4 million is a healthy return on an extensive remodel.A 1930s Spanish homeThe house sits on a cul-de-sac inside a gated community. It spans 4,825 square feet, with four bedrooms and five bathrooms. The 1930s Los Feliz residence was designed by Arthur Rowland Kelly, who also designed the Playboy Mansion. Ashley Benson was the third owner. For her, it wasn’t really love at first sight. “It was very old, and I really had to be open-minded [about] the potential,” the actor told Architectural Digest earlier. However, she was drawn to the Spanish-style home. “The outside felt like I was in Barcelona, or somewhere in Europe. And if I [did the work], I knew I would fall in love with it.”Benson purchased the house in 2020 and went for a thorough remodel before moving in. Her friend, interior designer Nicole Gordon, and architect John Farrace were in charge of the renovation. “She really wanted to respect the architecture and the integrity of the house. I think we both felt it was really special that she was [only] the third owner and that there hadn’t been a lot of bad additions,” Gordon told the publication. Benson wanted to preserve some of the original details. “The bones and all the interior architecture were amazing,” Gordon added.But she also made some personal changes. The kitchen cabinets are green, borrowing from the colour palette of the Polo Bar, the Ralph Lauren restaurant. The dining room is painted black from floor to ceiling and furnished in black to match. The primary bedroom has a dry bar stocked with whiskey. Benson has said it made her feel like she was staying in a hotel somewhere far away. Open one drawer, though, and the mystery is solved: it is mostly candy. The house also holds a speakeasy and a hair salon, two features that reflect her taste more than any resale instinct. Neither is the kind of addition most buyers would expect in a 1930s home, but they fit the house she wanted to live in.She sold the home after three yearsIn 2020, Benson paid $4.5 million for the house. Three years later, in July 2023, the property hit the market with an asking price of $9.49 million. Within a couple of weeks, the house sold for $8.5 million. This was below the original asking price but $4 million above what she paid. This gap is crucial. A sale price that far above the purchase price, after a three-year hold, represents a significant gain on any property. For the listing agents, this was a relatively easy sale. Along with the celebrity presence, the listing pitched the property as a blend of original charm and modern updates. The 360-degree views over Downtown Los Angeles, Griffith Park and the Observatory were among the other highlights.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: Jamia tensions rise: University shifts all classes online; AISA alleges assault on students during negotiations
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Amid ongoing student protests demanding the restoration of the students' union, Jamia Millia Islamia (JMI) on Saturday announced that classes
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Amid ongoing student protests demanding the restoration of the students' union, Jamia Millia Islamia (JMI) on Saturday announced that classes for all courses would be held online with immediate effect until further notice.The university, in a notice, said that the decision to shift classes online has been taken as a "precautionary measure" to ensure the safety and well-being of students."All Deans/Heads/Directors and faculty members as well as all bonafide students are hereby directed to adhere to the online class schedule and ensure regular participation in academic activities. All faculty members are requested to make the necessary arrangements for conducting classes through online platforms and to provide students with the required academic support and learning materials," the notice read.As this happened, the All India Students' Association (AISA) alleged that the Jamia administration began "assaulting students" in the midst of negotiations."The hunger strikers and the protest site are being attacked. This reveals the most brutal face of the Jamia administration," AISA said in a press release.This comes as the hunger strike of five Jamia students continued for the 13th day on Saturday. The students have been demanding restoration of their students' union (JMISU) while calling for the removal of the university's Chief Proctor for "cracking down" on protesters.Jasim Ali Khan, who has been on a hunger strike since the protest began, accused the university administration of launching a “crackdown” and demanded the revocation of students’ suspensions.Anas, another student protester, demanded that the show-cause notices issued by the proctor and disciplinary committee be revoked. He said the protests would continue until the university restored the students’ union.Addressing the ongoing controversy over graffiti on the university campus showcasing the "Free Kashmir" slogan, Anas argued that a narrative was being peddled to disrupt this peaceful protest. Urging the university admin to probe the matter, he asserted that protesters were not involved."A narrative is being peddled to (disrupt) the protest. We don't know whether the (university) administration or someone is peddling this. This is a matter of investigation since the responsibility for the security of Jamia lies with the admin. You check the cameras to see who is writing (such slogans) and clear the matter. The protesters and (hunger) strikers are absolutely not involved in this. The protest has been peaceful since day one and will remain the same in future," he told news agency ANI.Jamia students began their protest and hunger strike on October 12, demanding the restoration of the students’ union. articles.title: Seven missing after tall building collapses in Kenya's capital
articles.summary: Rescue efforts are under way to find people trapped under the block, which was still under construction when it buckled.
articles.body:
A search and rescue effort is under way to find seven people feared trapped under rubble after a building collapsed in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi.

Dramatic footage shows the bottom floor of the block, thought to have been 16 or 18 storeys, giving way before the rest of the building crumples, sending a plume of dust into the surrounding streets.

Dozens of builders had been working on the upper floors when it collapsed, but managed to emerge largely unscathed. Those missing were thought to have been in shops that had opened at the base of the building.

The incident has raised fresh concerns about construction standards and regulations in Kenya.

The block was under construction when it collapsed on Friday afternoon, with footage showing scaffolding still wrapped around the outside of the building. Officials said 11 shops had already opened on the bottom floors.

Interior ministry official Kipchumba Murkomen said 66 of the 67 construction workers in the building at the time had been able to get out unharmed, while the other had suffered injuries that were not life-threatening.

Images from the scene, in Nairobi's Eastleigh area, show the concrete floors of the building piled on top of one another, as rescue workers saw through metal to get to those believed to have been stuck underneath.

Rescue efforts have been complicated by concerns that excavation using diggers could limit the supply of air to those trapped, prompting emergency responders to cease using them, according to the Daily Nation newspaper.

Questions have emerged about why the building suddenly collapsed and whether it met planning regulations.

Kenya's National Construction Authority said in a statement that it had identified the company behind the development, as well as the architect and structural engineer, but did not say whether the site had been inspected before Friday.

Nairobi Governor Sakaja Johnson told local media that the owners of the building did not have the required paperwork for the building to be occupied.

He urged the national government to give local authorities greater powers to penalise "developers who disregard approved building plans and safety standards".

Building collapses are not uncommon in Nairobi, with poor construction or improper planning often cited as contributing factors.

articles.title: British woman dies after trying to rescue sons swept away at sea in the Bahamas
articles.summary: The children were subsequently rescued from the water, police say.
articles.body:
A woman has died after attempting to rescue her two sons when they were swept away while snorkelling in the Bahamas.

The Royal Bahamas Police Force said officers on the island of Bimini launched an investigation into the sudden death of a 36-year-old British woman on Tuesday.

The force said it believed the woman - believed to be from Stapleford in Nottinghamshire - was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.

In an attempt to rescue her sons, "the woman was also swept away", police said. The children were subsequently rescued from the water.

In a statement, posted on social media, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said: "According to the preliminary report, shortly after 10am, officers at the Alice Town police station received information that a female was unresponsive at the North Bimini Ferry Dock.

"Officers responded and, upon arrival, learned that the woman had been transported to the local clinic for medical attention, where she was subsequently pronounced dead by a local doctor despite efforts to save her life.

"Preliminary information indicates that the deceased was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.

"In an attempt to rescue her sons, the woman was also swept away.

"She was later rescued and transported to the ferry dock, where CPR was reportedly administered.

"Foul play is not suspected at this time.

"An autopsy will be conducted to assist in determining the exact cause of death."

A spokesperson for the Foreign Office added: "Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas.

"We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family."

articles.title: ‘Pengo was one of us’: Martial arts fighter, 26, identified by club as victim of suspected racist attack near Paris
articles.summary: The victim of Friday’s shooting in near Paris, which French President Emmanuel Macron described as a “racist terror attack,” was identified by his club as
articles.body: The victim of Friday’s shooting in near Paris, which French President Emmanuel Macron described as a “racist terror attack,” was identified by his club as 26-year-old Pengo Bossio Wangi, an amateur mixed martial arts fighter.The club announced his identity in a statement posted on Instagram, although French authorities have yet to publicly identify the victim.“Pengo was one of us. Nothing justifies taking a life this way,” the Atch Academy in Aubervilliers, north of Paris, said in an Instagram statement paying tribute to him.At least five other people, including a 12-year-old girl, were injured when a gunman opened fire from a vehicle at three locations in Trappes and La Verrière, about 30 km west of Paris, over a span of approximately 15 minutes."These people were targeted because of their skin colour or perceived religion, and for no other reason," Macron told reporters after meeting officials and residents in Trappes, adding that "there is no place for this in France."A suspect was arrested shortly after the shooting, and the National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor’s Office took over the investigation.The suspect was identified as Kévin T., born in 1987, although authorities have not disclosed his full surname. He had four previous convictions, which had been automatically expunged under French law.Investigators found a Sten-type submachine gun and a tear gas canister inside the suspect’s car. A search of his apartment also uncovered three gas cylinders and electrical wires connected to a timer, which authorities described as a “trap.”A member of the suspect’s immediate family was also taken into police custody following the fatal shooting.(With AP inputs)You use AI every day. articles.title: Yogurt shop murders fuel family questions about accomplice as rage lingers over wrongfully accused
articles.summary: Shawn Ayers, whose sister died in the 1991 Austin yogurt shop murders, co-founded the National Cold Case Center to help solve unsolved homicides.
articles.body: Nearly 34 years after his 13-year-old sister died during the 1991 Austin, Texas, yogurt shop massacre, Shawn Ayers and his wife, Angie, have launched a national cold case effort while still seeking answers about the attack and whether an accomplice is out there. Angie, along with Shawn, whose sister Amy was among four girls killed in the attack, have joined former prosecutors Mindy Montford and Anne Marie Schubert to establish the National Cold Case Center. The decades-long search for answers in Amy’s case inspired the couple to help establish the nonprofit, which helps to fund unsolved homicide investigations, train investigators and support victims’ families. FORENSIC GENEALOGY UNMASKS COLD CASE SUSPECT AS STRANGLER, SEXUAL PREDATOR DECADES LATER: OFFICIALS "Due to what we've gone through and seen, not only from our own experience, but from listening to other families struggle throughout this process," Angie told Fox News Digital. "Years ago, we had wanted to start a nonprofit." The Austin yogurt shop murders Amy, Jennifer Harbison and Eliza Thomas, both 17, and Jennifer’s sister, Sarah Harbison, 15, died in the attack at the I Can’t Believe It’s Yogurt! shop on West Anderson Lane on Dec. 6, 1991. On the night of the killings, Jennifer and Eliza were working the closing shift, while Sarah and Amy waited for them to finish so the four could head to a sleepover. Shortly before midnight, authorities received a report of a fire at the shop. The blaze and water from the sprinklers altered the crime scene and diluted evidence, according to FBI files. Inside, police discovered Sarah, Eliza and Jennifer stacked together in the shop’s storage room. They were stripped, gagged and bound with their own undergarments, and then shot in the back of the head with .22-caliber bullets. Investigators found Amy in a separate area with a ligature around her neck and burns covering up to 30% of her body, according to court documents. DNA FROM CHEWING GUM NAILS LONGTIME SEXUAL PREDATOR DECADES AFTER REIGN OF TERROR: REPORT FBI records described two gunshot wounds: an initial .22-caliber shot that missed Amy’s brain and a second shot from a .380-caliber pistol through her cheek and jawline. Investigators recovered a .380 cartridge casing in a floor drain. During the autopsy, officials recovered four .22-caliber bullets from the bodies. Killer identified The search for answers stretched across decades, combined with false confessions, arrests, convictions and appeals before DNA and ballistics evidence identified serial killer Robert Eugene Brashers in September 2025. Brashers fatally shot himself during a January 1999 police standoff in Missouri, leaving the families no chance to confront him at a murder trial. CALIFORNIA AUTHORITIES IDENTIFY FINAL UNKNOWN VICTIM OF ‘HAPPY FACE KILLER’ KEITH JESPERSON AFTER 34 YEARS Authorities had previously connected him to other violent crimes, including killings in South Carolina and Missouri. According to Austin police, Brashers used the same .380-caliber handgun in the yogurt shop murders to kill himself during the Missouri standoff. For the Ayers family, identifying Brashers didn’t answer whether someone else participated in the yogurt shop killings. Angie questioned whether another perpetrator may have been involved, since two weapons were used during the attacks. "I may be incorrect, but I don't think that I am," Angie told Fox News Digital. "There's never been an instance where he [Brashers] used both of those guns in his other cases." DETECTIVES' TRUE CRIME PODCAST TAKES FRESH SHOT AT KILLER WHO VANISHED AFTER CAUGHT-ON-CAMERA MURDER "There has been absolutely no definite answer on whether or not he was by himself, or had an accomplice. "So, to us, we still don't have all the answers, and knowing that this case is still ongoing, I don't think anyone can say that they know exactly what happened because we can't ask." Wrongful convictions Years before identifying Brashers, Austin investigators focused on four local teens: Robert Springsteen, Michael Scott, Maurice Pierce and Forrest Welborn. Austin police arrested all four in 1999. Springsteen and Scott confessed during police questioning but recanted before trial, saying investigators pressured them into giving false statements. Travis County juries convicted Springsteen of capital murder in 2001 and Scott in 2002. Springsteen received a death sentence, while Scott received life in prison. The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals overturned Springsteen’s conviction in 2006 and Scott’s in 2007. DNA testing failed to match any of the men to the crime scene. A judge released Springsteen and Scott in June 2009, and prosecutors moved to dismiss the charges that October. Pierce proclaimed innocence but implicated Welborn. In 1991, he wore a police wire and tried to coax Welborn into confessing. An Austin police officer reported that Welborn denied any involvement. Welborn later passed a polygraph test. Welborn never went to trial. When two grand juries failed to indict him, authorities dropped the case against him in 2000. By then, he had spent months behind bars. "I’m still really upset and mad at them. If they didn’t confess to something they didn’t do, we wouldn’t be here right now doing this today," Welborn told Texas Monthly. Austin police officers arrested Pierce in 1999 on capital murder charges. Prosecutors dismissed Pierce’s charges in 2003, citing insufficient evidence, after he spent more than three years in jail. In 2010, an Austin police officer fatally shot Pierce in 2010 following a traffic stop. Pierce fled the scene on foot and stabbed an officer in the neck with a knife, prompting authorities to open fire. Settlement After investigators linked Brashers to the killings, Travis County Judge Dayna Blazey declared the four men innocent on Feb. 19, 2026. Months later, the Austin City Council approved a $35 million settlement covering the three surviving men and Pierce’s family. Welborn initially rejected the city’s apology, saying that he lost an auto-repair business while incarcerated and endured years of public ostracism. "Their apology is not accepted," he told Texas Monthly. "Their apology means nothing to me." Welborn later said "it felt good" to have closure, although he wanted some of the detectives who worked the case "to go do some prison time." None of the detectives have faced criminal charges in the case, Texas Monthly reported. The Ayers couple said neither they nor the men or their relatives have contacted the other side. "We haven't reached out and they have not reached out," Angie said. Welborn could not immediately be reached for comment. The Austin Police Department and Travis County District Attorney’s Office did not respond to requests for comment by publication. Helping other families Their experience seeking answers in Amy’s case, and hearing other families describe similar struggles, prompted Shawn and Angie to consider starting a nonprofit years ago. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X "The frustrating part is being told no, but yet someone somewhere leaks the information and you're the last one to know when you should have been first and that is still happening today," Shawn told Fox News Digital, recalling his sister’s case. Their partnership with Montford began in 2017, when they met with prosecutors about the yogurt shop killings. Montford, a Travis County assistant district attorney at the time, promised to stay with them. "She made it a point to tell us that she was going to stick with us no matter what until the end," Angie said. articles.title: France braces for another day of mass protests as security on high alert
articles.summary: Several planned marches in major cities in France have been banned by authorities, provoking an uproar by rights groups.
articles.body:
Paris, France – More than 70,000 police officers and gendarmes are set to be deployed across France as the country braces for a new round of protests against deteriorating school conditions and the rising cost of living.

French authorities have made clear they are determined to prevent Saturday’s demonstrations from descending into the violence that erupted last weekend.

On October 17, protests that had been largely peaceful were marred by widespread looting, vandalism and clashes, with thousands of businesses damaged or ransacked. More than 2,000 people were taken into police custody, according to official figures.

To prevent a repeat, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said 20 percent more officers would be deployed than during the previous weekend.

The operation will also involve RAID, an elite police unit usually tasked with counterterrorism and other high-risk interventions. Nunez said its officers would not be directly involved in crowd control but would support other police operations.

Authorities have also adopted a highly restrictive approach to demonstrations on Saturday. President Emmanuel Macron said requests to protest from trade unions would be examined by local authorities, while demonstrations organised by other groups would be banned wherever possible.

In several cities, including Montpellier, Rouen and Nice, protests were prohibited in their downtown areas. In Lyon, demonstrations have been banned in the city centre, while in Marseille, a union-organised march has been authorised under strict conditions.

In Paris, a coalition of unions is due to lead a march from Porte d’Italie to Porte de Vincennes, along the Boulevards des Marechaux, between 1pm and 7pm, after the originally negotiated central route between Place de la Bastille and Place de la Nation was banned.

The ban – and the push of the march to the city’s edge – triggered an uproar.

“This security escalation comes at the expense of our freedoms, seriously endangering the right to demonstrate peacefully and raising fears of a further escalation of violence in our country,” said Amnesty International France.

In central Paris, businesses were shuttered and shop windows covered with protective panels, while some retailers hired private security. At least 24 metro stations were closed at the request of the police prefecture. Major cultural institutions, including the Louvre and the Musee d’Orsay, also closed for the day, while Art Basel Paris cancelled its weekend programme.

On Friday, Macron met representatives of the student movement for the first time since the protests began. He promised more teachers and a deep overhaul of Parcoursup, the admission system to access universities. But the meeting failed to defuse tensions, with student representatives calling for further mobilisation until the government presents concrete actions.

The protests began in mid-September, when high school students blockaded their schools over what they described as deteriorating conditions, including dilapidated buildings and teacher shortages, as well as what they see as an unfair system for accessing higher education.

The movement has since become a focal point for wider discontent over the cost of living, inequality and Macron’s presidency .

On October 17, more than half a million people took to the streets, following calls from student organisations and remnants of the Yellow Vest movement.

The unrest comes as France approaches a pivotal presidential election in six months. Macron, who is constitutionally barred from seeking a third consecutive term, will leave office in 2027.

The violence has also put a renewed focus on the far right, whose leading figure, Marine Le Pen, has long campaigned on a promise to restore law and order. Recent polls have placed her as the leading contender for the presidency by a wide margin.

Tensions are also expected in Orleans, where Le Pen’s National Rally is holding its party congress on Saturday, marking the start of its presidential campaign.

Authorities expect between 20,000 and 30,000 people to join a counter-demonstration against the far-right party, prompting a major security operation.

articles.title: MEA condemns deadly church attack in Jordan that killed eight
articles.summary: India on Saturday condemned a deadly attack on a Greek Orthodox church in Jordan that killed eight people and injured several others, expressing
articles.body: India on Saturday condemned a deadly attack on a Greek Orthodox church in Jordan that killed eight people and injured several others, expressing solidarity with the Jordanian government and people.In a statement, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said, "India unequivocally condemns the heinous attack at a Church in Karak, Jordan on 23rd October 2026, which resulted in the tragic loss of several innocent lives and injuries to many others. We extend our heartfelt condolences to the bereaved families and wish a swift recovery to those injured in this cowardly attack. India stands firmly with the Government and the friendly people of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan in this difficult hour. We also reaffirm our strong commitment to the fight against terrorism in all its forms and manifestations."External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar also condemned the attack and expressed condolences to the victims' families.The attack took place on Friday at a church in the village of Hammoud in the Karak governorate, where gunmen opened fire on a funeral procession. The death toll rose to eight on Saturday after one of the injured victims, who was in critical condition, died, Health Minister Ibrahim al-Bdour told AFP.Another 26 people remain hospitalised, including one in critical condition, the minister said.Jordan vows action after attackJordanian Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya described the shooting as a terrorist attack and said security forces were working to track down those responsible."A terrorist group has carried out a horrific act, one that is condemned in every respect, and the security services are working round the clock to track them down," he told a press conference.King Abdullah II, who visited the wounded at a hospital in Karak, also condemned the attack and said on X that the shooting "will be met with the harshest retaliation".Prime Minister Jafar Hassan ordered three days of national mourning beginning Friday, with flags to be flown at half-mast over government and public institutions.Karak is home to a significant Christian community in Jordan, a Muslim-majority country where Christians account for between two and three per cent of the population.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Mercury governs thought, speech and paperwork. Scorpio governs depth and the need for a straight answer. Retrograde motion turns the mind back toward matters that were never settled.Expect the mind to reopen old files. With both planets moving backwards in the same sign, questions about honesty and loyalty carry extra force. A relationship that has run on silence may show its gaps now.Revisit Without RushingGoing back over a matter does not mean acting on it today. Read the old message again. Check the figures. Mercury retrograde favours careful wording, since a hasty sentence can be misread on the first pass and again on the second.Say the Plain VersionTruth does not need force. articles.title: Deadly ‘racist’ attack in France: Are hate crimes rising in Europe?
articles.summary: Monitoring group reports more Muslims in Europe face racial discrimination as ‘terrorist’ attack kills one in France.
articles.body:
A gunman in northern France has killed one person and injured five, including a 12-year-old girl who was seriously wounded, in what authorities are calling a racially motivated “terrorist” attack.

The shooting on Friday was carried out as mounting and often violent cost-of-living protests grip the country with more demonstrations expected on Saturday.

President Emmanuel Macron called the shooting “a terrorist and racist attack”.

So what was behind this attack? And has there been a rise in Islamophobia in Europe?

About 10:30am (08:30 GMT) on Friday, a gunman drove through the towns of Trappes and La Verriere, a working class area on the outskirts of Paris with a large immigrant and Muslim population, and fired an automatic weapon randomly at a petrol station, a medical centre and a children’s playground.

The rampage lasted about 15 minutes before the suspect, identified as 39-year-old Kevin T, was arrested. Laurent Mazaury, the local MP, said the suspect told police he wanted to “kill foreigners”. He added: “I think we are facing a racist person.”

French media reported a young Black man was killed and a woman wearing a headscarf and a 12-year-old girl wearing a headscarf were among those shot and injured.

The man who was killed was identified as Pengo Bassio Wangi.

The girl, of North African descent, was shot eight times, according to her mother, and was transferred to a children’s hospital for surgery.

In a statement, prosecutors said of the five people injured, three were in critical condition.

How have the French authorities responded?

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told reporters on Friday that investigations are “ongoing but it is clearly a terrorist crime”.

Prosecutors said they were investigating whether the suspect had conspired with a “terrorist group” and added that a member of the gunman’s immediate “family circle” had also been taken into custody.

A local police chief told French media that the authorities had found an “older-style semiautomatic weapon” used in World War II in the suspect’s car as well as tear gas grenades.

The mayor of Trappes, Ali Rabeh, said the suspect was “firing at random” and wanted to cause a “bloodbath” in the communities, calling it “objectively a racist attack, probably Islamophobic”.

Writing on X, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the case was “very serious” and “all resources of the security forces and the judiciary are fully mobilised”.

The shooting comes at a moment of great tension in France as violent cost-of-living and student protests grip the country.

French authorities are to deploy 70,000 police officers on Saturday as protests, which some far-right voices have blamed on Muslim youths, are expected to continue.

What have the reactions to the shooting been?

Macron released a statement on Friday calling the “racist terrorist attack” a “turning point in the life of our Republic and our nation”.

“Tonight, I have reiterated the Nation’s support for all the victims and their families,” he said on X. “I have also reaffirmed our absolute determination to continue the fight against racism, in all its forms.”

Mayor Rabeh, who has Moroccan roots, said the people targeted “could just as easily have been my mother, my brothers or my sisters-in-law”.

“A 12-year-old girl is between life and death after being targeted by a volley of automatic gunfire in our country,” he said. “Her crime was probably being of colour.”

The girl’s mother told French broadcaster RTL: “How could anyone do this to a child?”

She questioned whether her daughter had been targeted because she was wearing a headscarf.

“She’s a child who was born in France, in Trappes,” she said. “She has the right to live in France, to make her life in France.”

The leader of the far-right anti-immigration National Rally party, Marine Le Pen, condemned the attack, calling it “barbaric”.

However, Muslim groups accused the populist right of creating a climate of hatred in the country with Islamophobic rhetoric. Most recently, Le Pen, who is campaigning for the French presidency, has proposed that women who wear the headscarf in public spaces should be fined.

Some members of the far right have also sought to blame Muslim young people for the violence taking place during ongoing protests, Farid Hafez, a senior researcher at Georgetown University’s The Bridge Initiative, which monitors incidents of Islamophobia in Europe, wrote in an article for Al Jazeera.

Last week, the European Parliament passed a resolution “on the need for an EU strategy to counter Islamist entryism and the influence of the Muslim Brotherhood network”. It was tabled by the centre-right European People’s Party and passed in a 381-167 vote with 15 abstentions.

“Symbolically, the resolution is a major victory for Europe’s right-wing anti-Muslim forces,” Hafez wrote. “It shows that the European Parliament has started abandoning any firewall against the far right as the centre right draws closer and closer to the far right.”

Rabeh said Friday’s shooting was a result of people “blaming all the ills of this society on Arab Muslims. All these comments cause deaths,” an apparent reference to the rhetoric of far-right political groups such as the National Rally. He denounced lawmakers who have made negative comments about Muslims as “criminals” who “ideologically weaponise those who are capable of committing crimes”.

The French Muslim Council blamed “the promoters of anti-Muslim hate speech who have blood on their hands”.

Are Islamophobic attacks on the rise in Europe, US?

Advocacy groups and monitors said they are.

In June, Amnesty International reported that Islamophobic violence in the United Kingdom has reached “ emergency levels ” with an escalating wave of hate crimes and targeted attacks, including rapes and firebombing of mosques.

The European Union’s Fundamental Rights Agency says racism against Muslims has risen in recent years and reported that one in two Muslims in Europe experience racial discrimination, especially when it comes to applying for jobs and housing.

In the UK, the monitoring group Tell MAMA reported 1,909 anti-Muslim cases last year, a 5 percent rise on the previous year, but said the true figure is likely to be much higher because many people don’t come forward.

The Council on American-Islamic Relations released a report on Friday condemning the attacks in France. It also revealed that reports of anti-Muslim bias are at an all-time high in the United States with California’s attorney general reporting a 54 percent rise in anti-Muslim hate crimes in 2025, from 24 to 38.
